💡 Key Takeaways
  • TorchNeuron provides a newly introduced native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium.
  • TorchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a new backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP.
  • 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TorchNeuron provides a newly introduced native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels natively support it, making it easier than ever to run models on Trainium and to share them on the HF hub.

TorchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a new backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP. Read the Pytorch blog to learn more about TorchNeuron.

Starting Oct. 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta. Researchers and developers will be able to install it with pip install torch-neuronx.

To date, the Hugging Face experience on AWS Trainium and Inferentia — AI chips designed respectively for cost-effective training and inference at scale — has been delivered through optimum-neuron. This library relies on the torch-neuronx package, which is based on PyTorch XLA. It was the natural choice at the time, but it meant thinking like a compiler: lazy tensors instead of eager execution, static shapes only, a recompilation for every graph break. Optimum Neuron existed to hide that complexity, and maintained custom code (modeling classes, trainers, etc) to do so.

It has been revealed that torchNeuron changes this. It integrates directly into PyTorch and exposes neuron as a native device, with eager execution, PyTorch's own distributed primitives (DTensor, FSDP2) and torch.compile.

Sources indicate that for the Hugging Face libraries, Trainium becomes a device like any other: Transformers, Diffusers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL run on it directly, with the same classes and scripts you would use on any other accelerator. From now on, we recommend that Neuron owners use these libraries directly instead of going through Optimum Neuron.

In a recent development, text generation is now natively supported in Transformers for a wide range of models. With TorchNeuron, 89% of the top 100 most-used text-generation model architectures are supported out of the box, compared to 46% with Optimum Neuron v0.4.5. You just need to pass the device_map=neuron argument in your code and your model will be moved to the Neuron devices.

Recent findings suggest that the following is an example of text-generation with tensor parallelism, which will enable to fully benefit from your Neuron instance. Note that it uses a static cache for generation as this is strongly recommended with Neuron to prevent frequent recompilations.

Recent findings suggest that now that Neuron is a native PyTorch device, training on Trainium uses the same Hugging Face libraries as any other accelerator: Transformers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL. You no longer need a dedicated trainer or a Neuron-specific fork of the model code. A standard TRL fine-tuning script runs on a Trainium instance with only a few Neuron-specific settings.

Here is a supervised fine-tuning script built on TRL's SFTTrainer. If you have fine-tuned a model with TRL on GPUs before, it should look familiar.

Parallelism is handled natively by Transformers. You put a DistributedConfig with the tensor-parallel (TP) and FSDP sizes in model_init_kwargs, SFTTrainer passes it to from_pretrained, and the model is sharded as its weights are loaded. The Trainer sees that the model is already distributed and does not wrap it again. You don't need an --fsdp flag or an Accelerate FSDP config.

It has been revealed that nothing in the script is tied to Trainium: the same code runs on any hardware. A few things are worth knowing when you run it on Trainium:.

It has been revealed that the command below releases training with torchrun, which starts one process per NeuronCore. TP_SIZE and FSDP_SIZE set the parallelism layout, and their product is the number of processes: here 4 x 8 = 32, matching --nproc_per_node. The 32 processes form a 4 x 8 grid. Tensor parallelism splits each layer across the 4 cores of a TP group, and FSDP shards the parameters, gradients and optimizer state across the 8 TP groups.

We ran it on 8 Trainium2 chips (32 NeuronCores), which is half a trn2.48xlarge instance.

Industry observers note that training runs to completion, and trainer.save_model writes a standard Transformers checkpoint. Nothing in it is tied to Neuron: you can push it to the Hugging Face Hub as is and load it on any other hardware.

Many pipelines from the Diffusers library are compatible with TorchNeuron in eager and compiled mode. FLUX.1-dev, FLUX.2, Qwen-Image, Qwen-Image-2.1 and H3 are also compatible with tensor parallelism to make the most of your Neuron devices. The following is an example showing how you can use TP:.

You can run this piece of code with: NEURON_LOGICAL_NC_CONFIG=2 torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 run.py.

Recent findings suggest that more and more pipleines will be compatible with TP. If a pipeline you like is not, you can also add support for it following this guide.

Recent findings suggest that make sure to check out the kernels from the Neuron team as more and more Neuron kernels will become available on the Hub to speed up your models. Neuron kernels can be written using the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI), which gives lower control to optimize operations. This way, users can run their own custom operations and share them on the hub.

You can use for example this kernel to speed up your vision transformers with up to a x2.4 speedup on Trainium!

Special thanks to the AWS team for their work on TorchNeuron and for their reactivity to our feedback to make the HF integration as good as possible.

Improving Human Impersonation, as the Web Closes Up Against AI

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1733 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Web scraping used to be a more casual affair: Robotic Process Automation (RPA) routines created on a write-once, run-many basis – humans recording their browsing actions, refining them through various automation processes, and setting them to run at intervals, unattended, in order to obtain data from websites that only want real humans (or paying clients) accessing them and their data – and which take measures to repel automated browsing of this kind.
  • In a recent development, of course, domains subject to this treatment often considered RPA to be more akin to ‘data exfiltration’ and/or ‘hacking’ than any definition of ‘browsing’.
  • Since publicly-available data has become a truly valuable resource for AI companies (rather than the insipid ‘Data is the latest gold’ rhetoric of ten years ago), at least 60% of reputable sites have been found to be repelling an AI crawler – a rise (in 2025) from 23%, two years earlier.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Web scraping used to be a more casual affair: Robotic Process Automation (RPA) routines created on a write-once, run-many basis – humans recording their browsing actions, refining them through various automation processes, and setting them to run at intervals, unattended, in order to obtain data from websites that only want real humans (or paying clients) accessing them and their data – and which take measures to repel automated browsing of this kind.

In a recent development, of course, domains subject to this treatment often considered RPA to be more akin to ‘data exfiltration’ and/or ‘hacking’ than any definition of ‘browsing’. Prior to the current era of AI, web scraping emerged from obscurity quite rarely, as a marginal form of pest; until LinkedIn introduced an ultimately-doomed lawsuit against HiQ Labs, an ‘intelligent automation’ provider, and one of many corporate concerns that challenged LinkedIn’s right to harvest publicly, profit privately.

Since publicly-available data has become a truly valuable resource for AI companies (rather than the insipid ‘Data is the latest gold’ rhetoric of ten years ago), at least 60% of reputable sites have been found to be repelling an AI crawler – a rise (in 2025) from 23%, two years earlier.

In practical terms, defending against any kind of web scraper is about pattern-matching, and looking for evidence of algorithmic access, such as screenshotting non-selectable text, or polling the CSS stylesheets, or the other underlying structures of a page.

These actions in themselves, no matter who or what executes them, are often considered evidence of automated processes rather than human interaction; personally – and especially at Yandex – I often have to complete CAPTCHAs because I make ‘uncommon’ or technical queries; and the more protective and protected domains are generally intolerant of anything but ‘mom ‘n pop’ baseline browsing behavior.

However, that’s still a relatively rare and heavy-handed experience. For the most part, anti-scraper logic and algorithms are looking not so much at the actions as for the way they are enacted – and especially for repetitive usage patterns for keyboard and mouse interaction. This could mean that a played-back RPA human interaction that works at first will shortly become blacklisted, because its lack of variation reveals it over time as a routine, and not a person.

Because of the growth of AI scraping, the tools of the RPA industry have suddenly become of great interest both to AI and intelligence companies that consider publicly available data ‘fair game’ in spite of any interstitial defenses (a stance theoretically supported by LinkedIn’s defeat in the aforementioned lawsuit – at least in the US); and the defending domains that in most (but not all) cases don’t have quite enough market capture to retain their profitable user base behind a login-wall, and would prefer to keep access open.

In the latter case, the companies have hardened themselves against the customary dedicated ‘headless’ browsers common in RPA, and against dedicated RPA frameworks such as Microsoft’s Playwright, and its derivatives and forks.

The security sector has taken an interest lately in whether AI-powered web agents can actually still be recognized by sites that are on the defensive against such activities. After all, these incursions may not be running on a CRON job, but neither are they ‘human’.

In this regard, a latest paper† from Canada proposes an AI-powered web agent designed to test the effectiveness of current anti-bot defenses. By combining a modified version of Chromium with AI models trained to reproduce human mouse and keyboard activity, the new system achieved access (non-rejection of browsing) in 89% of tests on a benchmark of protected websites – 12 percentage points above the best previously-published result:.

Comparative test results for bypassing eleven categories of web bot protection. Figures indicate successful page access as percentages, with test counts in parentheses. The new paper’s system, DarkAgent, achieved the highest overall score across 80 tests, compared with previously published results for nine other browser configurations. Source.

The system, dubbed DarkAgent, consists of Browsium, a customized Chromium browser engineered to conceal evidence of automated control; and Behavium, a framework incorporating two machine learning models: MouseGen, and KeyboardGen, which, together, simulate human interaction with the browser:.

Industry observers note that the DarkAgent workflow. Browsing decisions are translated into simulated human interactions, executed through Browsium’s native input mechanisms. The resulting page changes are fed back to the planning agent to determine its next action.

The architecture, shown above, addresses four categories of evidence available to bot detection systems, namely interaction patterns; browser and device characteristics; evidence of automated browser control; and network protocol characteristics.

The aforementioned KeyboardGen was trained on the Aalto keyboard dataset, derived from a study of 136 million keystrokes, to reproduce typing rhythms, errors and corrections. MouseGen was trained on the Boğaziçi Mouse Dynamics dataset, with additional scrolling data sourced from the Attentive Cursor dataset:.

Examples of mouse movements, in coordinate and interpreted form, from the Attentive Cursor Dataset. Source.

Both generators use Transformer architectures, while the browser modifications were implemented through conventional programming. OpenAI’s GPT-4.1 was used to decide which actions to perform during the benchmark tests.

According to recent reports, the browser’s reported identity and the simulated user behavior are coordinated throughout each session, so that the various signals presented to a website remain consistent with one another. To support this, a separate JavaScript-based environment within Chromium allows the agent to inspect web pages without exposing its presence to the website’s own scripts:.

Comparison of conventional browser automation (top), using the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) to inspect and control web pages, and the newly introduced paper’s approach (bottom), where a private communication channel reduces the evidence of automated activity visible to websites.

Recent findings suggest that the simulated mouse movements and keystrokes are then processed by the browser as genuine user input, with the same trusted status granted to physical mouse and keyboard activity. Variations in mouse trajectories and typing patterns, learned from recorded human activity, facilitate different sequences of movements and actin timings, reflecting the natural inconsistencies of human interaction.

DarkAgent was evaluated using Stealth Bench V1, a benchmark developed by Browser Use, comprising 80 short mouse and keyboard tasks on live websites, requiring no login and covering eleven categories of protection: Cloudflare; PerimeterX; DataDome; Akamai; reCAPTCHA; Kasada; Shape; GeeTest; hCaptcha; Temu; and (unspecified) site-specific anti-bot systems.

The tests were conducted in August 2026*, using geographically-matched residential proxies, with success measured solely by whether page access was obtained, and discounting task completion. Comparative results were drawn from earlier baseline tests conducted by the benchmark’s authors.

To establish the individual contributions of DarkAgent’s components, 30 browsing sessions were scheduled for each of 18 configurations on a website hosted by the researchers, with identical prompts, tasks, planning models, and limits on the number of actions.

For this, standard Chromium and Browsium were tested with and without Behavium, and with MouseGen and KeyboardGen enabled independently.

Additional comparisons were made with Firefox; Camoufox; the Playwright derivative Patchright; CloakBrowser; and publicly-available human behavior simulators Ghost Cursor; HumanTyping; and CloakBrowser’s Humanize.

The browsing sessions were evaluated using FP-Agent (an existing bot-detection system); additionally, JA4DB (a database of network connection fingerprints) was used to check whether the browser’s reported identity was consistent with its network activity.

Beyond the initial Stealth Bench V1 results presented earlier, all browsing sessions conducted without behavioral simulation were identified as automated by FP-Agent, while every session conducted with Behavium enabled in either Chromium or Browsium was classified as human:.

Bot detection results across 18 browser configurations, based on 30 sessions per configuration. P(Human) indicates the average probability of human activity assigned by FP-Agent, Verdict indicates the most frequent classification, and the final column identifies the browser engine inferred from the network connection.

Similar results were obtained with Ghost Cursor and CloakBrowser’s Humanize, indicative of a weakness in FP-Agent (which doesn’t examine how fast the mouse moves, or how its speed changes).

In a recent development, in AgentShield tests, all 139 form-filling sessions from the benchmark’s existing automated agents were flagged as bot activity, as were all ten sessions conducted with Browsium using standard automated input. With DarkAgent and CloakBrowser + Humanize, all ten trials per configuration were completed successfully without detection:.

It has been revealed that results of the AgentShield form-completion tests, showing successful submissions, bot detection rates, detection scores, mouse movements and keypress durations. DarkAgent and CloakBrowser + Humanize escaped detection, though DarkAgent’s keypress durations were considerably closer to those of human people.

In a recent development, when newly introduced fields appeared in the form, they were attended to by DarkAgent within an average of 3.74 seconds, compared to 4.72 seconds for human owners. The greater variation in human response times suggests, the authors contend, that bots could still be identified by the length and consistency of the pauses between actions.

Although this almost-impenetrable paper is not likely to gather many adherents to the cause, web scraping is one of the most interesting challenges for the dataset-builder and proponent of agentic AI.

However, it’s fast-becoming a Quixotic pursuit; even sites that may be indifferent to data acquisition routines are now likely to become defended against RPA and agentic AI in the very near future, simply because it is becoming a default position.

While data of the kind dealt with in this research can be extracted from human engagement farms in Asia, such data will inevitably form recognizable patterns in the aggregate, so that the routines that are part of them can be specifically blocked – a familiar pattern in a newly introduced cold war that’s starting to heat up.

Projecting the scenario to an extreme, truly effective RPA countermeasures could signal the wholesale revival of the crowdsourced worker – lately an eclipsed figure.

According to recent reports, † Titled ‘Are Web Agents Still Detectable? Stress-Testing Bot Defenses with Coordinated Evasion’.

* Relevant only because GPT4.1 was available then.

#162327. MPS in PyTorch 2.15

MPS in PyTorch 2.15

📅 20 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1371 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15!
  • A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face.
  • If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15! FP8 arrives on MPS, language-model decoding gets faster paths through linear layers and softmax and latest Metal kernels tackle some surprisingly expensive parts of audio, video and training workloads.

A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face. We contribute across PyTorch, and one of our focus areas is the MPS backend, where the goal is to make your Mac a first-class place to run and train PyTorch models. At the start of 2026, running even small models on MPS often meant working around unsupported operations, performance cliffs and unexpected memory growth. So we run real models from the Hugging Face Hub across language, image and video, find where MPS falls short and fix it upstream in PyTorch, more and more often by replacing MPSGraph with dedicated Metal kernels. Much of this post is the result of that work, done together with the PyTorch maintainers and community contributors.

If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:.

Industry observers note that you'll need an Apple silicon Mac with macOS 15 or later and Python 3.11 or later (see the 2.15 compatibility matrix). If your OS is too old or no Metal GPU is available, the MPS availability check now tells you why.

To try the release candidate in a separate environment:.

FP8 gives you another way to save memory on your Mac. PyTorch 2.15 adds torch.float8_e4m3fn tensors on MPS: one byte per value, half the storage of FP16 or BF16.

You can multiply these tensors with F.scaled_mm, which supports both tensorwise and rowwise scaling. Here's a small example with one scale per tensor:.

Recent findings suggest that every LLM has a prefill phase and a decode phase. During decode, each upcoming token goes through the model as a single row, so the major matrix multiplications turn into matrix-vector products. PyTorch 2.15 speeds up both kinds of layers that dominate this step: dense linear layers and mixture-of-experts layers.

Sources indicate that MPS has had GEMV kernels for torch.mm since 2.14, but F.linear still went through MPSGraph. PyTorch 2.15 connects them to F.linear, so the common [1, 1, hidden_size] decoding input uses them directly, with eligible bias additions fused in. Across 96 BF16 layer shapes from real models, that's a 1.23× geometric-mean speedup. The biggest wins land on small projections, such as the gates in MoE models, where the old path left most of the memory bandwidth unused. Large layers and LM heads were already close to bandwidth-bound, so they stay near 1×.

Recent findings suggest that A mixture-of-experts layer sends different numbers of tokens to each expert. Grouped matmul handles those uneven groups in a single operation, and 2.15 gives MPS a native implementation.

Sources indicate that in 2.14, grouped matmul copied the group offsets to the CPU and looped over the groups. The newly introduced Metal kernels read the offsets directly on the GPU, using Metal Performance Primitives where available and a separate Metal path elsewhere. Small groups, the common case during decoding, get their own kernel as well.

For example, 64 tokens can be split into groups of 16, 32, and 16:.

Industry observers note that the decoding kernel highlights up directly in token throughput. On an M3 Ultra with torch.compile, MoE models generate about 1.3× more tokens per second:.

Working with complex tensors gets easier. complex64 LU factorization, LU solve and triangular solve now run on MPS, which also unlocks the operations and gradients built on them, such as complex determinants. Here's a small system solved directly on the GPU:.

Recent findings suggest that small matrices get fast kernels too. For camera geometry and image transformations, batches of FP32 matrices up to 4 × 4 are inverted in a single Metal kernel that combines factorization and solving. Larger problems get attention as well: QR uses blocked updates, and triangular solves turn much of their work into efficient matrix multiplication.

Gated DeltaNet workloads get a dedicated fast path for batches of 16 × 16, 32 × 32 and 64 × 64 FP32 triangular systems with at least eight right-hand sides.

It has been revealed that SVD is also more robust at numerical extremes. It now correctly handles very small singular values, very large or very small input magnitudes and basis completion with full_matrices=True, which in turn makes pseudoinverse and least-squares results more reliable.

Recent findings suggest that audio models, video decoders and training loops have their own expensive operations. This release gives several of them upcoming paths through Metal:.

It has been revealed that token sampling gets faster in 2.15 as well. softmax and log_softmax now run on dedicated Metal kernels, and large vocabularies benefit the most: an FP32 softmax over a [1, 128256] row of logits drops from 57 µs to 7 µs, about 8× faster than the MPSGraph version. The speedup holds across other common vocabulary sizes:.

Industry observers note that one of the most striking results in this release comes from the constant-padding change. The VAE decode in Wan-AI/Wan2.2-TI2V-5B-Diffusers makes 8,764 padding calls over a full 28-tile decode. With padding on Metal, peak driver memory drops from about 270 GiB to 8 GiB:.

You can now pick which MPS stream runs your work, directly from Python. torch.mps.Stream and the torch.mps.stream context manager provide the interface, and Tensor.record_stream lets the allocator track a tensor's use on another stream.

Here's a small example that sends work to a separate stream and synchronizes before reading the result:.

Recent findings suggest that several more operations now run on MPS: torch.frexp, torch.logspace, torch.take and Tensor.put_, torch.heaviside, torch.special.laguerre_polynomial_l and unsigned-integer comparisons. logspace doesn't yet support integer or boolean outputs with more than one element.

Attention gets a correctness fix too: the MPS math implementation of scaled dot-product attention now handles batch and head broadcasting correctly.

Work on 2.16 is already well underway. Some of the changes below have landed on main and are available in the nightlies; others are still in review, so details may change before the release.

According to recent reports, once a model's decode path no longer contains any MPSGraph ops, the GPU only starts on a token after the CPU has finished encoding all of its kernels. PyTorch 2.16 commits the command buffer every 16 kernels, so the GPU gets to work while the CPU is still encoding the rest. For compiled BF16 decoding at a 2048-token context:.

Sources indicate that scaled dot-product attention is dropping MPSGraph completely: every shape will run on Metal kernels, with dedicated vector kernels for decoding and Metal Performance Primitives for half-precision prefill on newer macOS versions. The shapes that used to fall back to MPSGraph benefit the most. On an M5 Pro, decoding with grouped-query attention (32 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 80, 4K context) drops from 465 µs to 65 µs, and a 4K × 4K prefill with head dim 40 goes from 42 ms to 6 ms.

The move away from MPSGraph continues. Batch norm forward and backward are in progress, while MSE loss (up to 12× faster on small inputs), std_mean and var_mean (up to 4× faster) and bincount have already landed. bincount is the most dramatic: when most values fall into a single bin, counting 4 million integers used to take 6.8 seconds and now takes half a millisecond.

Bundled shaders will build for Metal 3.1 by default, with Metal 4 versions compiled only for the kernels that need them. That shrinks libtorch_cpu.dylib by about 25%, from 384 MiB to 287 MiB, and lays the groundwork for Metal 4.1 shaders with faster matmuls and native FP8 matrix multiplication.

It has been revealed that pyTorch 2.15 brings FP8 to the Mac, faster LLM decoding for dense and MoE models, more linear algebra on the GPU and a long list of operations moved from MPSGraph to dedicated Metal kernels. Give the release candidate a try!

A substantial thank you to Nikita Shulga, Kurt Mohler and Aaron Gokaslan for reviewing much of this work, and to everyone who contributed to MPS in this release.

Slack and ClickUp overlap more than a simple chat-versus-tasks comparison suggests: Slack has Lists and workflows, while ClickUp includes Chat and collaborative Docs. The decision is which environment should organize the team’s daily work.

Choose Slack when your biggest need is communication across departments and the tools you already use. Choose ClickUp when tasks, dependencies, time, and reporting need one accountable home. We prefer ClickUp as the delivery system for a project-heavy team, with Slack retained when its wider communication network already has value.

Both products appear in our best AI collaboration tools guide. This comparison evaluates where each belongs in a real team workflow, including where using them together is more useful than replacing one with the other.

Consider a product team preparing a website launch. Design must finish before development, copy needs approval, and analytics must be ready before release. A marketing lead needs a quick answer about launch risk, while individual contributors need to know what to do next.

Sources indicate that slack is a natural place to create the launch channel, bring design and engineering into the same thread, and capture the decision behind a change. A Slack list can assign small follow-ups with dates and status. A canvas can keep the brief and key links visible, reducing the time new participants spend asking for context.

Recent findings suggest that clickUp gives the launch a more explicit delivery structure. Tasks can carry an assignee, due date, status, and custom fields; subtasks separate work that belongs under a larger deliverable. Dependencies make the relationship between design, development, and approval more visible. A manager can move between a task list and a schedule view without reconstructing the strategy from messages.

Sources indicate that for a small, straightforward launch, Slack Lists may be enough. Our recommendation moves toward ClickUp when there are repeated handoffs, several releases, or a need to track effort and report progress consistently. ClickUp’s flexibility brings setup work of its own: too many statuses and custom fields make a simple project harder to use.

In Slack, a useful AI request starts with work the team has already discussed: summarize the open questions, explain a decision, or prepare a brief for someone joining the project. Slackbot’s value comes from the relevant context it can access, not from replacing an accountable owner. The official example below shows research being organized into a canvas; it is a vendor product example, not a result from our own test.

Sources indicate that clickUp Brain can work with project context, and the action-item menu shown below illustrates the connection between writing and follow-up work. The useful result is a proposed set of actions that a team can assign and refine. For the launch example, we would keep those actions in the project so that a summary and the delivery record do not drift apart.

Industry observers note that slack is the stronger choice when the question is who said what, why a decision changed, or which colleague needs to join the discussion. ClickUp is the stronger starting point when the output needs to become managed project work. Neither AI output settles a dependency or commits a deadline on its own; a project owner still needs to approve the change.

Strategy choice matters for this workflow. Slack Free and Pro provide a limited Slackbot preview; Business+ includes 15 messages per member each week, with additional usage available through the applicable credit arrangement. It has been revealed that choose Slack if colleagues need a better way to coordinate, ask questions, and act on information from several business tools. Its strongest case is a team whose work already spans departments and needs a shared communication layer.

Choose ClickUp if work has dependencies, time tracking, repeated assignments, or reporting needs that outgrow a lightweight list. Its integrated Chat may also reduce the need for a separate messenger within a self-contained project team.

We recommend Slack for teams whose coordination spans many departments and business tools, and ClickUp for teams whose main problem is executing projects reliably. For an established Slack organization, connecting ClickUp is often a better move than migrating every conversation just to improve task management.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last November, we introduced AnyLanguageModel on this blog: a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework that lets you choose the model and provider your app uses. We heard from app developers who were curious about local models but weren't always sure how to get started. They also wanted to avoid the added complexity of supporting multiple inference providers. AnyLanguageModel grew out of that feedback.

It has been revealed that local and hosted inference each have their strengths, and both have a role in building this new generation of intelligent apps. A shared API makes it easier to choose the right model for each task.

A year and dozens of releases later, AnyLanguageModel 1.0 is out, along with swift-huggingface 1.0 and swift-xet 1.0.

Here's what changed, and what's next:.

Recent findings suggest that the core idea of AnyLanguageModel remains the same: use the Foundation Models API with the model that fits your app. To get started, change your import statement:.

The same session code then works with the system model, with open-weight models through llama.cpp, MLX, and Core ML, and with the hosted providers below.

Over the past year, we've added several major features:.

On OS 27, AnyLanguageModel also works with any model that conforms to Foundation Models' LanguageModel protocol, including Core AI models.

Alongside AnyLanguageModel, we've built out swift-huggingface and swift-xet to bring accelerated model downloads from the Hub to Swift apps.

Sources indicate that support for hosted models expanded this year, too. AnyLanguageModel now supports:.

With Inference Providers, you can use open-weight models that are too significant to run on the device with the same session code:.

Hosted providers get the same features as local models: guided generation, tool calling with streaming, and token usage on responses.

In a recent development, reasoning is now part of the transcript too. When you switch providers, reasoning blocks are automatically omitted from requests if the new provider can't replay them.

In a recent development, API keys come from a closure instead of a string, so your app can fetch short-lived tokens from your own server. The README explains when to let people bring their own keys and when to route requests through a proxy.

AnyLanguageModel also runs on Linux, so the same code can work on a server.

While we've made local models easier to use, the models themselves have become more capable, making the small ones a good place to start. Here are some of the most downloaded models on the Hub right now:.

In a recent development, the first two fit on an iPhone, and Qwen3.8 27B runs on a Mac with 32 GB of memory or more. Selecting the MLX model takes one line:.

And if you have four maxed-out Mac Studios handy, GLM-5.3 from Z.ai takes about 1.5 TB in BF16. For the rest of us, it's available through Inference Providers.

If you're upgrading an existing app, see the migration guidance in the AnyLanguageModel, swift-huggingface, and swift-xet release notes for help updating your code.

Community feedback and contributions have shaped several of our major features. Thank you to everyone who contributed for helping make AnyLanguageModel more useful to app developers.

Industry observers note that language models have proven to be a powerful tool for building intelligence into products. They're also one of many kinds of models developers can put to work. We're excited to bring the same approach to more capabilities: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of models running on the device. Coming soon: models that decide, and models that listen.

  • Distillation uses answers generated by a more capable model to train another system.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Reuters reported on November 26, 2026 that Z.ai had fallen behind schedule on GLM-5.5, its next flagship designed with roughly 3 trillion parameters, a measure of model size, while Moonshot AI had begun distilling from Google and Meta models as training data from OpenAI and Anthropic models became harder to obtain.

Distillation uses answers generated by a more capable model to train another system. A person familiar with Moonshot’s operations said anti-distillation safeguards had also slowed its development, and that Google’s and Meta’s latest releases had made their models attractive alternative data sources. Moonshot is also seeking substitute computing: a separate source said it had intensified efforts to rent capacity in Europe, corroborating earlier CNBC reporting, and planned to approach Chinese chipmakers about training on their processors.

Industry observers note that two people familiar with the matter said Z.ai had planned to release GLM-5.5 in November 2026. One of them said increasingly effective anti-distillation safeguards were partly responsible for the hold-up and that fresh US computing restrictions could push the launch into the first quarter of 2027 or later, despite the earlier goal of finishing training and releasing it by the end of 2026. Z.ai, Moonshot, Google and Meta did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The disclosures put simultaneous pressure on the resources behind Chinese developers’ low-cost challenge to US rivals: outputs from more capable models and overseas access to advanced chips. Anti-distillation measures constrain unauthorized extraction of model outputs, while the new licensing rule targets overseas arrangements that let developers use Nvidia processors without importing them.

Recent findings suggest that moonshot is particularly exposed to the new US Commerce Department rule because it rents computing power to train its models and prioritizes overseas providers, a person with knowledge of its operations noted. The rule took effect on November 19, 2026 and imposes licensing requirements for covered computing arrangements at data centers outside the US above a threshold roughly equivalent to 750 Nvidia H100 chips. Operators already providing covered services before the rule took effect have 90 days to obtain licenses.

Sources indicate that A person with knowledge of Moonshot’s operations noted domestic computing capacity could not fully replace its overseas supply if access were cut off entirely, a scenario that could stretch its usual six-month interval between major releases to 12 months or longer and push Kimi K4 to around mid-2027. Moonshot released Kimi K2 in July 2025, K2.5 in January 2026, and K3 in July 2026.

Sources indicate that Z.ai announced GLM-5.4 on November 23, 2026, describing it in the model’s technical release as its first flagship built on a Loop Transformer. The architecture reruns a shared block of layers to refine internal states without adding parameters. The 750-billion-parameter model loops 28 layers from the GLM-5 base for two iterations; Z.ai adapted an already pretrained base through continued training rather than starting from scratch.

It has been revealed that Z.ai states the design reaches intelligence comparable to models with 2 trillion to 3 trillion parameters. To control deployment costs, the second pass reuses the first pass’s attention indices and combines shared and sliding-window key-value caches, which store prior context, rather than creating another full-context cache.

According to recent reports, the tech giant also acknowledged that GLM-5.4 can enter excessively long reasoning loops, although it remarked the resulting reflection and self-correction improve accuracy beyond the model’s parameter count. The model is available through Z.ai’s chat and coding products; API access is listed as coming soon, and open weights are planned after safety hardening.

In Anthropic’s September 2026 threat-intelligence report, the firm defines illicit distillation as industrial-scale, covert extraction without authorization and attributes more than 23 million exchanges to Moonshot between May and July 2026 and more than 3.4 million to Zhipu, branded outside China as Z.ai, over 17 days in June and July 2026.

According to recent reports, anthropic stated Moonshot silently relayed customer requests to Claude and used fraudulent proxy accounts and cross-session replay techniques to extract reasoning transcripts for training, while Zhipu used Claude to clean and normalize harvested transcripts, judge model outputs, filter training data, and support other post-training work. Anthropic’s layered defenses combine proxy-network attribution, extraction classifiers, account bans, identity checks, and summarized or encrypted reasoning intended to make stolen transcripts less useful.

Moonshot previously told China’s National Business Daily in July 2026 that Kimi K3’s gains came from original architectural changes, rejecting suggestions that they resulted from distillation.

GLM-5.4 demonstrates how architectural efficiency can extend an existing model, but it does not resolve the constraints around the next generation. The reported GLM-5.5 and Kimi K4 schedules are exposed to tightening access to large-scale computing and training data drawn from rival models, pressures that reusing a pretrained base cannot fully address.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Grafana Begins Its Biggest UI Refresh Since Version 7.

Nov 27, 2026 3 min read.

Grafana Labs has introduced the first phase of its biggest visual refresh since Grafana 7, bringing updated themes, more consistent interface components, and improved visual hierarchy to its observability platform. Introduced as part of Grafana 13.3, the refresh is now available in public preview across Grafana Cloud and self-managed deployments.

The changes address a growing problem as Grafana has expanded: years of rapid feature development have created design inconsistencies, competing visual elements, and different interaction patterns across the platform. Rather than introducing a complete redesign, Grafana is standardising its existing interface while retaining familiar navigation and plugin compatibility.

The longer-term objective is to make the platform easier to use as observability workflows increasingly incorporate AI assistants and agent-driven interactions.

Grafana's extensive growth has brought support for a broad range of observability use cases, but this has also introduced what the company describes as design debt. Different parts of the interface have evolved independently, resulting in inconsistent visual cues, component variations, and interaction patterns.

It has been revealed that the design refresh is intended to address these inconsistencies without slowing the platform's continued development. Grafana wants users to learn an interaction pattern once and apply that knowledge consistently across dashboards, panels, drawers, and other parts of the interface.

The work has also been influenced by the development of Grafana Assistant and Assistant Workspace, which introduced new interaction patterns for AI-powered workflows and prompted the design team to reconsider the platform's visual language.

According to recent reports, newly introduced default light and dark themes use redesigned colour palettes intended to improve accessibility. Grafana has also reduced the number of available component variations, helping standardise how common interface elements behave.

Typography, borders, shadows and visual layering have been updated to create a clearer information hierarchy. The intention is to reduce competing visual elements and make it easier for users to identify vital information when investigating incidents or exploring data.

These changes extend across fundamental interface components, including cards, panels, and drawers. Rather than simply applying a new visual style, Grafana is revisiting the underlying design primitives so that the interface remains consistent as the product evolves.

An interesting motivation behind the refresh is Grafana's view that traditional graphical interfaces will increasingly coexist with terminal-based and agentic chat interactions.

As more workflows become accessible through AI assistants, the remaining graphical interactions need to be particularly clear and predictable. Users should be able to understand the information presented, recognise notable changes and move between workflows without having to relearn different interface conventions.

According to recent reports, this makes visual consistency more than a cosmetic exercise. It becomes part of ensuring that engineers can work effectively across both traditional observability interfaces and newer AI-assisted experiences.

Grafana is deliberately introducing the refresh in phases, allowing people and contributors to adapt while providing feedback before further changes are made.

It has been revealed that importantly, the organization describes this as a visual refresh rather than a complete redesign. Existing navigation remains unchanged, and the update introduces no breaking changes for plugins.

Industry observers note that self-managed users can enable the new styling through the grafana.visualDesignRefresh feature toggle and can switch back to the previous appearance if required. Grafana Cloud users can also access the public preview.

The organization has encouraged feedback through its community Slack and an in-app survey, using early adoption and user responses to guide subsequent iterations.

Other observability platforms, including Datadog and Fresh Relic, have also invested in simplifying how engineers navigate increasingly complex monitoring environments. Grafana's challenge is particularly interesting given its open-source ecosystem, where plugins and contributions introduce additional interface requirements.

The refresh reflects a broader product engineering principle: as platforms grow, maintaining consistency becomes as notable as introducing new functionality.

For observability tools, where engineers often work under pressure during production incidents, reducing cognitive overhead can directly improve how promptly they find and interpret relevant information.

Sources indicate that grafana's refresh is therefore less about changing how the platform works and more about making its growing capabilities easier to understand and use. As AI increasingly changes how engineers interact with observability systems, a clear and consistent graphical experience remains an important part of the overall design.

📅 20 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (862 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that if you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX.
  • Industry observers note that TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit.
  • It has been revealed that TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that if you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX. With TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend, TPU is now just another device. It opens up native support of TPU in the Hugging Face ecosystem. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels run natively on TPU. Pick a model from the Hub, send it to "tpu", and you're done.

Industry observers note that TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit. TPUs are Google's own AI accelerators. They are chips built for one job: the matrix math that neural networks spend most of their time on. Google has been designing them for about ten years, and uses them to train and serve its own models, including Gemini.

It has been revealed that TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips. They shine when you need a lot of compute, for training or for serving at scale.

In a recent development, the catch has always been software. The TPU stack grew up around TensorFlow and JAX, and PyTorch owners had to work harder to get in.

Sources indicate that until now, running PyTorch on TPUs meant going through PyTorch/XLA (torch_xla). It worked, but it had its quirks. Tensors were lazy (the tensors, not you), so your code didn't always run when you thought it did. Small changes could trigger graph recompilations, and debugging was hard to reason about.

Recent findings suggest that to make life easier, we built Optimum TPU. It gave Hugging Face models inference and training support on TPUs. Now that TorchTPU brings native support, Optimum TPU is not required anymore to run Hugging Face models with Transformers and Diffusers.

TorchTPU adds TPU as a latest backend to PyTorch. You write regular PyTorch code. It comes with Pallas kernels tuned for TPUs, support for distributed training, and a torch.compile integration for when you want more speed. Installing it on a TPU VM takes one command:.

The extra index gives you the CPU build of torch. Without it, pip pulls the much bigger CUDA build, which you don't need on a TPU.

Transformers v5 was built around one idea: be the source of truth for model definitions, so they can run anywhere. "Anywhere" now includes TPUs. To load a model on a TPU, pass device_map="tpu". That's it.

In a recent development, the model runs in eager mode by default. You can also use torch.compile for better performance, or run it in a distributed setup.

Sources indicate that TPU is now a first-class device in Diffusers. For prototyping or debugging, eager mode only needs pipe.to("tpu"). For deployment, compiled mode adds one compile call. Your pipelines and code stay the same, and there's no TPU fork to maintain.

The first call compiles, and every call after that with the same image size reuses the graph.

It has been revealed that models too big for one chip? Pass a TensorParallelConfig to from_pretrained and the transformer is sharded across chips as it loads, so the full model never has to fit in one place. Many popular pipelines support it out of the box, and the ones that don't are just a tp_plan away. The Diffusers TPU guide has the full recipe.

Here are some examples run on a Cloud TPU v6e-4:.

TP=4 (each model split across four chips) · bf16 · batch 1.

The Kernels Hub has ready-to-use TPU kernels. Load one with the Kernels library and give your model a speed boost.

TPU kernels are written in Pallas, which gives you low-level control over the hardware. You can also bring in kernels from the Tokamax library. Here is a ragged-dot kernel from Tokamax plugged into a Mixture-of-Experts model:.

In a recent development, the bigger the batch, the bigger the win. At batch size 64, decoding is 21.5× faster on Qwen3-30B-A3B and 12.8× faster on Gemma 4 26B-A4B.

It has been revealed that decode throughput on a TPU v6e-8, Hub kernel vs. the default implementation.

We're continuously improving TPU support in transformers by running the library test suite. We are working to add a nightly CI on TPU and make the results available in the (transformers dashboard)[https://huggingface.co/spaces/transformers-community/transformers-ci-dashboard].

In a recent development, the Transformers CI dashboard, with TPU results next to other accelerators. Work in progress!

It's not all green yet, and we're fine with that. Of the tests that run on TPU, 96.5% pass. Every failure we find becomes a small repro script and an issue on the TorchTPU repo. So far we have reported 34 problems, and 19 are already fixed. Running on TPU also caught a few bugs in Transformers itself, like in StaticCache and the Qwen3 tensor-parallel prepares. We fixed those upstream.

If something breaks on TPU, we want to find out before you do.

In a recent development, TPUs are no longer a side quest for PyTorch users. Install TorchTPU, grab a model from the Hub, and send it to "tpu".

Recent findings suggest that we can't wait to see what you build 🤗. If you hit a problem, open an glitch and tell us about it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NEURA Robotics announced on November 27, 2026 that it has signed a memorandum of understanding with the Government of Aragón and Costa Group to establish NEURA Gym Aragón and a surrounding Physical AI Model Zone, with investment planned in the double-digit millions of euros.

Sources indicate that the partners are targeting a mid-2027 opening, with NEURA Robotics taking the leading investment role. Their aim is to help companies in agriculture, agri-food, logistics, automotive and manufacturing develop robotic applications and position Physical AI, which enables robots to use perception and learned capabilities for physical tasks, as a new source of economic growth in Aragón and Spain.

NEURA will build and operate the Gym, providing technology and tools that connect robotics, AI models, simulation and its Neuraverse platform. Companies will bring their own tasks and process knowledge, train and test applications on different robot systems, and assess performance before deployment.

The shared infrastructure is intended for small and medium-sized businesses as well as larger industrial groups, universities and technology centres. NEURA’s premise is that reliable Physical AI applications require experience with real materials, tools and processes; the Gym is meant to bring that training environment closer to the employees who understand the work.

Sources indicate that through Neuraverse, participating partners will retain control of their manufacturer-specific knowledge and robotic skills. They can keep a skill private or license it under agreed commercial terms, making control of industrial expertise part of the project’s commercial model. NEURA founder and CEO David Reger summarized the incentive: “A company that develops a valuable skill should benefit when others use it.”.

Sources indicate that the Physical AI Model Zone will extend that work into designated environments where partners can test applications under representative operating conditions. Potential settings include industrial operations and selected service environments, and the Zone is intended to show how an application performs beyond a training cell before wider deployment.

The Zone’s scope and locations, as well as participation by other autonomous systems, remain to be defined with the relevant partners and authorities. Any extension into publicly accessible areas will require appropriate permissions and safety measures, placing limits on how testing can move into shared public spaces.

Fraga-based Costa Group, an Aragonese agri-food group, will serve as the industrial anchor partner. Its agricultural and industrial operations will provide practical challenges, use cases and operational expertise for developing and evaluating applications, while its regional network will help connect the work with businesses and employees. The partners will initially explore applications intended to improve productivity and reduce physically demanding or repetitive work.

The Government of Aragón will support skills development, coordination with relevant authorities, and connections with regional companies, universities, research institutes and business associations. Universities in Aragón, including the University of Zaragoza, will contribute research expertise and methods, provide opportunities for students and researchers, and support talent training through joint projects and activities.

Sources indicate that the partners expect the project to create skilled roles in Gym operations, user training and support, and application development, as well as opportunities for regional suppliers and technical service providers. Aragón will also join NEURA’s expanding Gym network, connecting regional teams and companies with other European and international locations.

That network is intended to make regional expertise commercially useful beyond its place of origin through deployment, technical services and skill licensing. For Aragón, the project’s central test is whether shared training and representative-condition testing can turn local process knowledge into deployable, licensable robotic skills, giving smaller companies access to development infrastructure while they retain control of their expertise.

Tech Report: The Prototype Paradox: What to Do When AI-Built Apps Outgrow the People Who Made Them

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2611 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Picture a Friday afternoon in a mid-sized manufacturer’s planning team.
  • According to recent reports, that story is now ordinary.
  • Industry observers note that I don’t think that’s something to be alarmed about.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Picture a Friday afternoon in a mid-sized manufacturer’s planning team. A supply planner is tired of pulling three exports, cleaning them by hand and pasting them into a tracker. She opens an AI coding assistant and describes what she wants. Two hours later she has a small web app that pulls the data, flags late purchase orders and suggests which ones to expedite. It works. On Monday she shows it to two colleagues. By the end of the month, a dozen people across planning and procurement use it every morning. Nobody in IT knows it exists.

According to recent reports, that story is now ordinary. The barrier to building software has nearly disappeared, and the evidence reveals how fast people are taking advantage of it. According to Verizon’s 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report, 45% of employees now regularly use AI tools on work devices, three times the 15% recorded in 2025. Much of that use happens outside official channels. Gartner’s Q1 2026 Global Labor Market Survey of more than 12,000 employees and managers in 40 countries found that 88% of workers who have an employer-provided AI tool also use a personal one for work.

Industry observers note that I don’t think that’s something to be alarmed about. It’s mostly a sign of real demand. But it creates a problem that most organizations haven’t named yet. The difficult question is no longer whether people can build useful software with AI. It’s what happens after they do.

Sources indicate that enterprise software usually enters an organization through a door: a procurement process, a security review, an architecture decision. AI-built tools come in through a different route. They begin as personal conveniences and become shared infrastructure gradually, without anyone deciding that they should.

Industry observers note that I think of this as an invisible graduation. A personal tool becomes a team tool when the first colleague bookmarks it. It becomes an operational tool when someone gives it a live database connection instead of a spreadsheet export. It becomes critical when a process starts to depend on it, and the old manual workaround is forgotten.

Sources indicate that each step seems minor. Taken together, they turn a weekend project into something the business runs on, with none of the controls that would normally come with that role. Survey data indicates this is already widespread. In BlackFog’s survey of 2,000 UK and US employees, 51% mentioned they had connected or integrated AI tools with other work systems or apps without IT approval or oversight. The same research found 60% were willing to accept security risks with unsanctioned AI tools in order to work faster or meet deadlines.

Industry observers note that we have seen this pattern before. In the 1990s and 2000s, spreadsheets and desktop databases built by business customers became the hidden backbone of finance, risk and operations at many companies. Some of the most expensive operational failures of that period came from those end-user tools: models nobody had reviewed, formulas nobody could trace, and files whose authors had long since moved on. AI-built apps are the same phenomenon with more power. A spreadsheet can only do what its formulas allow. An AI-built app can call APIs, write to databases and send emails.

Industry observers note that in most business functions, an ungoverned tool is mainly a governance and audit problem. In supply chain operations, it’s a continuity risk, because supply chain sits underneath almost everything else the business does.

According to recent reports, think about where the planner’s expedite tool ends up being used. During a port disruption or a supplier shortfall, it’s the first thing the team opens. Its recommendations shape which orders are pushed, which customers are told to expect delays and how inventory moves between locations. If it breaks at that point, or quietly produces wrong answers, the effects don’t stay within planning. They reach customer service, finance, manufacturing and eventually the customer.

Industry observers note that the blast radius of a tool depends on how many decisions downstream of it rely on its outputs, not on how sophisticated it is. In supply chain, that number tends to be large and to grow without anyone noticing.

When AI-built tools fail to make the transition into enterprise operations, it’s usually because of two kinds of debt that the original builder never had a reason to pay down.

In a recent development, the first is security and compliance debt. Apps generated from a handful of prompts often have weak or absent access control, have never had a security review, and were never assessed against frameworks such as SOC 2 that the rest of the stack must meet. This isn’t simply a matter of careless builders. The underlying models have well-documented weaknesses. In its 2025 GenAI Code Security Report, Veracode tested more than 100 large language models on 80 curated coding tasks and found that, although the code worked, it introduced security vulnerabilities in 45% of cases. More worrying for anyone expecting the problem to disappear by itself, Veracode found that even as models got better at producing syntactically correct code, their security performance stayed flat over time.

The second is knowledge debt, and it gets far less attention. All software needs maintenance. When a tool is built by one person through a conversation with an AI, the only real documentation is in that person’s head, and often not even there, since they may never have read the generated code closely. The tool becomes tribal knowledge. When its builder changes roles, goes on leave or leaves the manufacturer, nobody can fix it, extend it or say with confidence what it does. Knowledge debt grows with adoption: each upcoming user increases the cost of the day the tool stops working.

For this reason, I expect a large share of the vibe-coding activity inside enterprises today to end up as throwaway work. That doesn’t make it a waste. Many of these tools are excellent prototypes. They prove a need exists, define requirements more clearly than any workshop could, and show what users actually value. But a prototype that proves a need is a different thing from a system built to meet it.

Industry observers note that banning these tools would be a mistake, and it probably wouldn’t work. TrustedTech’s Shadow AI in the Workplace report found that almost one-third of employees stated they would keep using AI tools even if workplace rules banned them and disciplinary action was possible. A ban pushes the activity out of sight. It doesn’t stop it.

A more useful approach is to treat AI-built tools as positions on a ladder, where each rung has a clear set of expectations:.

According to recent reports, rung 1: Personal sandbox. One user, read-only access to data that user already owns, such as a personal export. The tool informs; it doesn’t act. Here the right policy is to leave it alone. These tools are where experimentation happens, and the cost of failure is one person’s afternoon.

Rung 2: Shared insight. A few users, still read-only, still informing rather than acting. The risk is no longer a security breach. It’s a wrong answer spreading across a team. Minimum expectations: a named owner, a short description of what the tool does and where its data comes from, and a check that someone other than the builder can run it.

Industry observers note that rung 3: Connected. The tool has a live connection to systems such as ERP, planning or customer data, even if it only reads. That changes the security picture entirely. The tool now needs proper access control, credentials management and a security review equivalent to what you would require of any third-party software holding the same data.

Sources indicate that rung 4: Acting. The tool writes back to systems of record, changes dates or quantities, or sends messages to suppliers or customers. That makes it production software in every sense, and it belongs on a governed platform with auditability, change control and a team responsible for supporting it.

Sources indicate that two questions determine where a tool sits and when it needs to move up: Who depends on it? and What can it touch? The number of customers is the clearest indicator of what a failure would cost. Data access and the ability to act determine how bad that failure could be. One additional test overrides the rest: if nobody other than the builder could maintain the tool tomorrow, it’s already a liability on any rung above the first.

The aim isn’t to stop tools from climbing the ladder. Tools that climb are the ones proving their value. The aim is to ensure the controls keep up with the climb, rather than finding out after an incident that a Rung 1 tool has been operating at Rung 4 for six months.

For a long time, enterprise software decisions followed a reasonably settled rule. Building was slow and expensive, so you bought anything that didn’t differentiate your business. AI has unsettled that rule because building has become fast and cheap.

Industry observers note that but this reasoning confuses the cost of creating software with the cost of owning it. AI has sharply reduced the cost of the first version of an application. It has done much less to reduce the cost of securing it, scaling it, supporting consumers, responding to audits and continuing to develop it over years as requirements change. Those are the costs that make software ownership expensive, and generating code promptly doesn’t make them smaller.

According to recent reports, so the question should change. “Can we build this?” now almost always has the answer yes. The more useful question is: “Do we want to own this permanently?”.

If a capability genuinely distinguishes your business, owning it may well be worth it, and AI makes building it more feasible than it has ever been. If it’s operational plumbing that many other companies also need, such as demand sensing, inventory reconciliation or supplier collaboration, your engineers’ time is probably better used elsewhere. In those areas, it makes sense to work with providers who carry the security, compliance and maintenance burden every day and can respond to your requirements promptly. The economics of AI favor building in more cases than before. They don’t make every build a good idea.

My own engineering team learned a version of this firsthand. When we’ve given AI a loose prompt and accepted the result at face value, we’ve sometimes spent longer understanding and fixing the code than it would have taken to write it carefully from the start.

We aren’t the only ones. In a randomized controlled trial run by the research nonprofit METR, 16 experienced developers worked on real tasks in projects they knew well. When they were allowed to use AI tools, they took 19% longer on average, even though beforehand they had predicted AI would speed them up by 24%. The researchers were careful to say the result doesn’t mean AI tools are useless, and the tools have improved since. But the difference between perceived and actual productivity is the important lesson, and it matches what we’ve seen.

I think the cause is a shortcut in the design process. Building software used to mean writing a detailed specification and handing it to a developer. Now AI can produce the specification itself, and because it looks polished, people often don’t read it closely. It looks fine at a glance. The problems are in the details, and detail skipped at design time comes back later as rework.

The same is true for business processes. AI can produce workflows that look very convincing. Humans still have to do the due diligence: get into the details, check the logic and settle the design with a person involved. Once that’s done, AI can run the process reliably every day. The design step is the one part you can’t yet hand over to AI.

It has been revealed that the same discipline applies to the AI automation that does reach production. Start with tasks that are repetitive and deterministic, where the correct output follows reliably from the inputs. These can still be complex. What matters is that they don’t depend on judgment. Aim for automation that is right almost all the time, close to 99%, so that consumers come to trust it.

According to recent reports, over-ambition has a cost that’s easy to underestimate. Imagine an automated process that’s right 60% of the time. It’s tempting to describe that as “automating 60% of the work.” In practice, users can’t tell which 60% is right without checking all of it. They end up reviewing every output, investigating the 40% that’s wrong and correcting it, often with less context than if they’d done the task themselves. An automation at that accuracy can easily generate more work than it eliminates, and it damages users’ willingness to trust the next automation you introduce.

Production AI should run inside explicit policies: guardrails that keep outputs within predefined ranges, and clear rules about which actions can run automatically and which need human review. An AI that proposes reorder quantities might be allowed to act alone on changes within a narrow tolerance and be required to send anything outside that range to a planner. As models get better and a track record builds up, those guardrails can be relaxed. Autonomy should be earned through demonstrated reliability, not granted in advance.

For organizations that want to move from reacting to these tools to managing them deliberately, here is a practical sequence:.

It has been revealed that vibe coding isn’t the problem. It’s one of the fastest ways an organization has ever had to discover what its people actually need. The mistake is treating a fast prototype as a finished enterprise system or letting it become one by default because no one stopped to decide.

According to recent reports, the organizations that scale AI well will be the ones that spot the difference early. They’ll keep personal tools personal, move shared and operational tools onto governed foundations before something breaks, and decide what to build or buy based on what they’re prepared to own for the long term, not on how quickly something can be built. In supply chain, where every function depends on the initiative being right, that discipline is what separates innovation from fragility.
