Profiling TorchNeuron (Part 1): System-level profiling on AWS Trainium.

📅 21 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1286 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow.
  • This post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience.
  • Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow. In Part 1 of this series, you will learn how to systematically analyze inference performance and identify where the time is spent.

This post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience. The walkthrough uses AWS Trainium, a purpose-built AI chip for deep learning training and inference workloads, and TorchNeuron, its open source native PyTorch backend. TorchNeuron supports standard PyTorch workflows on Trainium, including eager execution, torch.compile, and standard PyTorch APIs, with minimal code changes. Additionally, TorchNeuron integrates with Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) to enable custom operators and performance optimization for Trainium hardware. By the end, you should know:.

Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.

The Neuron backend uses PyTorch's PrivateUse1 extension point. This mechanism lets an accelerator integrate with the framework without adding a dedicated dispatch key such as cuda. The torch_neuronx package works with upstream PyTorch to register Neuron as a native backend for PyTorch code. For details about this extension mechanism, see Facilitating Latest Backend Integration by PrivateUse1.

You use two objects to profile a Neuron workload:.

According to recent reports, the modes parameter selects the data streams to capture, such as device instructions and runtime traces. The capture_enabled_for_nc parameter selects the NeuronCores to trace. Setting correlate_device_time=True propagates device time from the trace into the key_averages() table, where you can compare CPU and Neuron device time. For the complete parameter reference and available ProfileMode values, see the NeuronConfig Profile Modes documentation.

Neuron Explorer is a browser-based viewer for the system trace, device timeline, and per-engine breakdown. You can access it through an SSH tunnel or the Visual Studio Code extension. In this post, you use Explorer to confirm what key_averages() reports numerically and inspect what happens between dispatches.

Sources indicate that after profiling, the output directory contains the system trace and, when you capture device data, matched .neff and .ntff files. The Neuron Executable File Format (NEFF) contains the compiled Neuron executable, while the matching NTFF contains its hardware instruction trace. The files share a numeric hash that identifies them as a pair. To open the profile in Neuron Explorer, upload the complete output directory for a system or combined profile. For a device-only profile, upload the matching .neff and .ntff files individually. See Step 5: Upload your profile for the UI and command-line instructions.

For this first analysis, you profile RMSNorm, a small operation with a clear sequence of arithmetic and reduction operations.

You profile three implementations of the same operation:.

The scripts use the same inputs, profiler configuration, and schedule so the results are directly comparable.

All scripts to reproduce this work are available in the torch-neuronx examples directory.

Start by writing RMSNorm with individual PyTorch operations. Each line maps to one or more ATen operations and can create intermediate tensors.

Call the profiler with two arguments required for the Neuron backend:.

Sources indicate that the schedule uses wait=2, warmup=1, and active=1 across four prof.step() calls. This records one warm iteration without including initial setup overhead.

Industry observers note that call torch.neuron.synchronize() inside the profiler loop. Without this synchronization, the profiler can export before the device finishes and leave the Neuron time column empty.

In a recent development, after profiling finishes, inspect the key_averages() table. Sort by self_privateuse1_time_total to place the operations with the highest device cost first. The table shown here is filtered to the RMSNorm operations that report Neuron device time. The full key_averages() output also includes CPU-side events such as allocations and host-to-device transfers.

The key averages table reveals that three aten::mul calls account for the largest share of Neuron device time.

It has been revealed that the table indicates which ATen operations ran, how often they ran, and how much time they spent on the CPU and Neuron device. aten::mul has the highest total device time because the function performs three multiplications.

Industry observers note that each row maps directly to the function. aten::mul runs for x * x, x * rms, and the final multiplication by weight. aten::mean reduces the last dimension. aten::add adds the epsilon value and triggers a host-to-device copy because the scalar starts on the CPU. aten::rsqrt computes the reciprocal square root.

Neuron Explorer follows an aten::mul operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to execution on the Neuron hardware lanes.

In Explorer, time flows from left to right and the event lifecycle flows from top to bottom. Each ATen operation follows the same pattern: creation in the framework lane, scheduling in the runtime lane as nrta_execute_schedule, and device execution in the hardware lane as nc_exec_running.

The system trace view organizes events into lanes. In the Default grouping mode, labels follow the pattern instance/PID/subsystem/identifier:.

According to recent reports, in eager mode, each operation runs independently. Use the dependency chain viewer to follow aten::mul.Tensor from the framework layer through runtime scheduling to device execution.

The dependency chain viewer highlights the lifecycle of one operation across the framework, runtime, and hardware lanes.

Replace the individual operations with PyTorch's built-in rms_norm function. Neuron lowers the operation to one fused kernel:.

The fused RMSNorm appears as one device operation in the key averages table.

The fused RMSNorm follows one framework-to-hardware path instead of dispatching each arithmetic operation separately.

Sources indicate that in the naive implementation, each operation crosses the dispatch boundary independently and follows its own framework-to-runtime-to-hardware path. In the fused implementation, one Python call covers the complete computation. The trace contains one dispatch and one hardware event, with no gaps between component operations.

For the final example, compile the original naive RMSNorm function with torch.compile.

According to recent reports, with @torch.compile(backend="neuron"), TorchDynamo captures the Python bytecode as an FX graph and AOTAutograd lowers it to ATen operations. The Neuron backend receives the complete graph instead of dispatching each operation separately. It fuses the operations, optimizes memory access, and compiles the graph into a single NEFF artifact. The artifact runs as one hardware dispatch.

The compiled function appears as one Torch-Compiled Region in the key averages table.

The compiled graph follows one path through runtime scheduling and hardware execution.

It has been revealed that the table highlights one device execution, as in Profile 2, but the code takes a different path. Instead of calling a purpose-built fused operation, the compiler discovers the fusion from the original Python function. In this run, the Neuron time is comparable to torch.rms_norm, at 375 μs compared with 403 μs.

Both torch.rms_norm and torch.compile fuse RMSNorm into one kernel dispatch. In these runs, either approach takes about one-sixth of the naive implementation's device time. Fusion removes the gaps between hardware executions and avoids materializing intermediate values such as x_sq and mean_sq between separately dispatched operations.

key_averages() shows which operations consume device time, while its full output also reveals CPU-side setup and transfers. Explorer provides the corresponding visual trace. You can follow one operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to hardware execution and see the gaps that fusion removes.

You can use the same workflow on larger models: find a hotspot in the table, verify it in the trace, and then determine whether a fused operation or torch.compile can reduce its cost.

Industry observers note that in Part 2, we will move into the device-level profile. You open the NEFF, inspect the TensorEngine, VectorEngine, and direct memory access (DMA) breakdown, and place the kernel on the roofline to determine whether it is compute-bound or memory-bound.

Special thanks to Aritra Roy Gosthipaty for the inspiration to begin this series, and to my peers Pinak Panigrahi, Samir Araujo, Akhil Azhikodan, Esha Lakhotia and the rest for reviewing!

#162308. Grok Bots Attempt to Access Corporate Data Without User Approval

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1276 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Darkreading ↗ Open Full Page

Grok Bots Attempt to Access Corporate Data Without User Approval

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1276 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Darkreading

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Two AI agents, separately over a five-day period, autonomously tried to access connected applications, including Google Calendar, Gmail, Slack, and GitHub, without account owner permission.
  • Grok Bots attempted to access corporate applications without their owners' approval or knowledge, presenting yet another security challenge for enterprises as AI agents become increasingly autonomous.
  • In a recent development, researchers at NewCore identified 31 unprompted attempts by two xAI Grok Bots to access connected corporate applications over a five-day period, including Google Calendar, Gmail, Slack, GitHub, and Notion, according to the findings of an investigation published today.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two AI agents, separately over a five-day period, autonomously tried to access connected applications, including Google Calendar, Gmail, Slack, and GitHub, without account owner permission.

Grok Bots attempted to access corporate applications without their owners' approval or knowledge, presenting yet another security challenge for enterprises as AI agents become increasingly autonomous.

In a recent development, researchers at NewCore identified 31 unprompted attempts by two xAI Grok Bots to access connected corporate applications over a five-day period, including Google Calendar, Gmail, Slack, GitHub, and Notion, according to the findings of an investigation published today. In one case, the bot continued making background requests even after its owner had declined offers for recurring check-ins four times.

The requests were not approved and did not reach the underlying corporate data: NewCore had placed a security gateway between the agents and the applications, requiring human approval for each request.

"Over five days, two Grok Bots on NewCore employee accounts made 31 requests to calendar, email, Slack, GitHub and Notion while nobody was talking to them, some with the laptop shut," Ido Hoorvitch, security research team lead at NewCore, wrote in the report.

Related:Critical PHP Flaws Allow Code Execution, but Don't Panic 'PHP2Shell'-Style.

According to recent reports, one bot repeatedly attempted to retrieve Google Calendar events in the evening, overnight, and the following day, despite there being no active conversation with its owner. In a second case, another bot attempted to access Notion's calendar tools before Google Calendar had even been connected. It continued making requests while its owner's laptop was closed and asleep.

The investigation began as an internal experiment at NewCore, which wanted to understand how autonomous AI agents behave when connected to real corporate systems. The company earlier this year provided employees with enterprise Grok Bot accounts and connected the agents to corporate services, including email, calendars, Notion, and other business applications.

However, NewCore put a handbrake in place: It did not give the agents unrestricted, standing access to organization data. Instead, requests had to pass through its Model Context Protocol (MCP) gateway. The gateway sent an approval notification to the employee who owned the account whenever a Grok Bot tried to access an application. If a request was not approved within three minutes, it automatically expired and was denied, Hoorvitch stated.

According to recent reports, "We did it because we had no way to audit why an agent reaches for data, and until we do, the gate stays closed by default," he wrote. Ultimately, this security control allowed NewCore to observe and reconstruct the bots' background activity.

Related:Cursor Traces Malicious Claude Code Extensions to Third-Party Breach.

According to recent reports, the first sign that something was amiss came after an employee used Grok Bot to retrieve their daily calendar, approving the request through the gateway as expected. Later that evening, however, the gateway recorded further calendar access attempts, despite the employee no longer interacting with the bot.

Industry observers note that this led investigators to uncover repeated attempts by Grok agents to access corporate applications without any corresponding user interaction. Moreover, when one bot was asked whether it had made the gateway calls, it said it had not, Hoorvitch said. The requests did not appear in the bot's chat history.

In a recent development, "It was telling the truth. … That is the part to sit with," he wrote. "An agent that cannot account for its own actions is not a bug report. It is a finding.".

NewCore contacted xAI about its findings and mentioned the company's support team confirmed that the activity was not the result of a software vulnerability or an exploit, but was part of Grok Bot's built-in background check-in functionality.

"These are built-in background check-ins by the primary bot, during a check-in the bot looks at its connected sources, and there is no user or admin setting to turn them off," Hoorvitch wrote, relaying the response from xAI support.

Related:F-Secure Identifies 26 Ways AI Can Harm Consumers, and Where to Stop Them.

According to NewCore, xAI also said that customers seeking to stop the check-ins could send the vendor a list of employee sign-in addresses. NewCore said it had not received an official response from xAI's media team at the time the report was published.

Sources indicate that the lack of a user- or administrator-facing setting to disable background check-ins, or to control which connected tools they can use, creates a visibility and governance challenge for security teams. Employees may not know when an AI agent is accessing connected applications, while the agent itself may not retain a record of its server-initiated activity in the chat history visible to its owner.

"The danger is not that the model goes rogue," Hoorvitch explains to Dark Reading. "The concern is that we hand agents standing credentials and then let someone else decide when they act. The owner thinks the bot works when they talk to it. The vendor thinks a helpful bot checks in on its own. The model does what the platform tells it in that turn, not what the owner would have said.".

Though "nobody in that chain is malicious," he notes, "the result is still a bot reading your inbox at 7:46 a.m. while you are asleep.".

The distinction matters because all 31 unattended requests identified by NewCore were read operations, such as retrieving calendar events or searching messages, Hoorvitch explains. None resulted in data being accessed, because the gateway blocked them. However, the same connected tool sets included capabilities to take actions, such as sending email, modifying calendar events, and posting Slack messages. NewCore warned that the same background processes could pose a greater risk if they were to invoke those write-capable tools.

Recent findings suggest that in NewCore's investigation, its MCP gateway blocked all 31 unattended requests. The manufacturer argues that organizations need similar independent controls to set and enforce policies on AI agents operating within their systems.

"Put the decision outside the agent," Hoorvitch indicates. "Route every agent tool call through something you own, like the NewCore MCP Gateway, where the owner's policy decides what goes through and every call is logged whether or not the agent remembers it.".

It has been revealed that newCore also recommends that organizations immediately inventory the agents connected to corporate tools, identify which applications and data they can reach, and assign an owner to each. Security teams should review not only approved activity but also requests that were denied or left unanswered, since these can reveal what agents attempt to do without user involvement.

"Most teams cannot answer that today," Hoorvitch states, "and you cannot govern what you cannot list.".

📅 21 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2202 w)

How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications

📅 21 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2202 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications.
  • In a recent development, in an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens.
  • The tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications.

In a recent development, in an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens. This article previews some results from the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon: how we specialized the vocabulary around the cost of each token rather than its frequency, and cut measured inference cost by 77% without changing the base model.

The tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone. For a model specialized in a single domain, it can be one of the largest cost levers, and it is set before any training step.

According to recent reports, one of the systems we run in production is an automated grader for Portuguese essays, built on Qwen3-4B. It receives the essay, the prompt and the supporting texts, and returns a JSON assessment with a grade and a comment for each competency.

The model was already small, at 4 billion parameters, and had already been trained for the task. Its tokenizer, however, was still the original Qwen3-4B one, built for many languages and many kinds of text. In the grader, it was used for a single language, Portuguese, and a single response format. That had two costs: the text the grader writes on every request took more tokens than it needed, and at every generated token the model scored a vocabulary of 151,669 entries, including many this task almost never uses.

According to recent reports, we rebuilt that vocabulary with a method we call VocabX, keeping the same base model, the same data and the same training recipe. The numbers in this article come from the current version of the paper, still under review, and may change before publication.

Sources indicate that the leading language models read and write in tokens, and the tokenizer decides how text becomes tokens. The tokenizers of the leading general-purpose models are trained on large collections of text from many domains and languages, from source code to contracts to Chinese. For a general-purpose model, that choice makes sense.

For a model used in a single domain, it creates two kinds of waste at once.

According to recent reports, the first is fragmentation. The tokenizer splits into many pieces exactly what the domain repeats most. In the grader, every response starts with the same JSON envelope, the same competency names, the same evaluation phrases. In contracts, it is the boilerplate clauses. In code, the identifiers. Each of these sequences costs several tokens where one would do, and the model pays for every one of them on every request.

The second is excess. The vocabulary carries tens of thousands of entries the domain never uses, and the model computes a score for all of them at every token it generates. A model tuned to grade American school biology exams will almost never write in Chinese, yet it computes the probability of every Chinese-language token at every step. The vocabulary splits into many pieces what the domain repeats most, and carries entries the domain never uses.

In a recent development, the natural reaction is to count tokens and try to reduce the count. But the count is not the bill.

It has been revealed that to see why a generated token costs more, it helps to look at how inference works. It has two phases. In prefill, the model processes the whole input in a single pass through the network: each weight read from GPU memory is reused for every input token, and the limit is compute. In decode, the model generates the response one token at a time, and each token needs a full pass. Each weight read is used only a few times, and the GPU spends most of its time waiting for data to arrive from memory: the limit becomes memory bandwidth.

Sources indicate that this effect is strongest exactly where we operate: small models served with moderate batches. Batching requests splits the weight reads across them and eases the problem, but does not solve it. At every decode step, the model also reads the KV cache, the attention memory that holds the context already processed and grows with it. In the case we measured, the grader, a generated token costs 7.4 times a token read, but the ratio varies with the hardware, the problem, the batch size, the context length and other factors, and it can be larger than that. In general, the direction holds: generating costs more than reading.

In a recent development, think of a shipping manufacturer that charges per box, but charges seven times more for outgoing boxes than for incoming ones. Reducing the total number of boxes helps. Reducing the outgoing boxes helps seven times more. A method that compresses input and output equally misses most of the possible savings.

The third component of the bill is the vocabulary itself. The model's last layer, the LM head, turns the internal state into a score for every possible token. To do that, it holds one row of parameters per vocabulary entry. In a model the size of Qwen3-4B, that matrix accounts for almost 10% of the parameters. It is a share that large models absorb without noticing, but it weighs on a small model.

And the cost is not paid only once. The input layer looks up only the row of the token being read, but the LM head reads and multiplies the entire matrix for every generated token. Since decode is already memory-bound, every extra row is more data to move at every step. An entry the domain never uses costs exactly the same as a frequent one. That is why adding tokens can lower the count and raise the bill at the same time. VocabX does not include this term in its selection criterion, but it controls vocabulary size in two steps: the sub-word merge replaces the base vocabulary with a smaller, domain-specific one, and macros enter under a fixed budget. In the grader, the output layer went from about 152,000 to about 65,000 rows.

Sources indicate that adapting a model's vocabulary is not a new idea. Reference methods in the literature, such as fast vocabulary transfer (FVT), multi-word tokenization (MWT) and Liquid AI's in-place tokenizer expansion (in-place BPE), which continues BPE training from the original vocabulary, already reduce fragmentation. When we tested them on our problem, we found two limitations.

They choose tokens by frequency, not by cost. An expression that appears often in the input is worth more to them than one that appears less often in the response, even if the second is the more expensive one to serve.

They work on a single layer. They either adjust how words are cut into pieces, or merge whole phrases into one token. None of these three does both under the same criterion. And the grader's biggest waste was precisely in long, repeated spans such as the JSON envelope, which a sub-word method only reaches after merging each part, one by one.

VocabX addresses both limitations, plus a third problem that appears on the obvious path to solving the first.

Industry observers note that first, we changed the question. Instead of asking how many tokens a candidate saves, we ask how much cost and time it saves. Each eliminated token is multiplied by the price of the field it appears in: system prompt, user message or model response. In the case we measured, the grader, a token saved in the response is worth 7.4 times one saved in the input, and the vocabulary is built accordingly.

Sources indicate that second, we work on both layers at once. Back to the shipping tech giant: you can cut boxes by packing each item better, or by recognizing that the same twelve-item kit ships every week and sending the kit in a single box. VocabX does both. At the sub-word layer, it rebuilds how domain words are cut into pieces. At the multi-word layer, it looks for whole spans that repeat, from short expressions to full lines and JSON envelopes, and turns each into a single token, which we call a macro token. Both layers are chosen under the same cost criterion, each with its own budget.

To find these spans, we use five miners, automatic searches for spans that repeat across the corpus, each specialized in one kind of repetition: long words, whole lines, expressions, complete sentences, and structures with punctuation such as JSON and tags. Averaged over eight corpora, the last one contributed the most, and on code it alone accounted for 17.5 points. Without all five, token reduction on the grader would drop by 55.6 points.

Third, we estimate what the sample cannot see. Choosing tokens by cost requires knowing how much each candidate still saves after the ones already chosen. Measuring that exactly would require reprocessing the entire corpus after every choice, tens of thousands of times. A common way to do this at scale is to measure on a sample of documents, and then a candidate absent from the sample gets zero gain.

An expression that appears 37 times in 50,000 documents indicates up in a 400-document sample only about 26% of the time. In a contracts corpus, only 16.6% of the candidates appear in a 400-document sample; the rest are never evaluated.

Sources indicate that A candidate's gain has two parts. One is how much it saves over the entire corpus, and that can be counted exactly, without a sample. The other is how much of that saving is not yet covered by the tokens already chosen, and only that part needs to be estimated. For candidates the sample cannot see, we use a statistical estimate based on the behavior of the ones it can see, instead of zero. A candidate that is rare in the sample but frequent in the corpus is back in the running.

That change alone, with the same sample and the same budget, raised token reduction on a contracts corpus from 44.7% to 52.8%.

To measure the real effect, we trained seven versions of the grader with the same base model, the same data, the same recipe and the same seed. The only difference between them is the tokenizer. All of them ran the same 500 requests on the same test machine, with an RTX 5090 GPU and the vLLM inference server, and cost was calculated from measured runtime.

The model's response dropped from 350 to 101 tokens on average. Cost dropped 77.0%. Quality, measured by the bench score, which combines grading accuracy and the accuracy of screening off-topic or rule-breaking essays, rose from 0.703 to 0.810.

Sources indicate that getting there required a course correction. The first version of the vocabulary fused each competency's grade with the surrounding JSON into a single macro token. It was the most compact option, but quality dropped: its bench score was 0.689, below the production grader's 0.703. With the grade inside the macro, each combination of grade and structure became a different variant of the same token, and the model chose both in a single step. Giving the grade its own token cost 2 extra tokens per response, raised the bench score to 0.810 and, in the measurement, was even cheaper: a 77.0% reduction, against 73.3% for the fused version.

The lesson applies beyond the grader. Compression has a cost when the compressed span carries the very decision the model exists to make. The goal is not the cheapest possible vocabulary, but the cheapest one that preserves the tokens that matter.

Industry observers note that to find out whether the gain was specific to our case, we compared VocabX with the three reference methods on five public domains (contracts, medical papers, scientific papers, news and Python code) and three model families (Qwen3, Llama-3.1 and Gemma-3). All methods used the same mining and test documents, and the same vocabulary ceiling.

VocabX compressed more than the strongest reference method in all fifteen combinations, by 1.2 to 9.3 points. In estimated inference cost, the pruned version of VocabX also led in all fifteen, with average margins of 10.2 points on Qwen3, 7.5 on Llama-3.1 and 13.6 on Gemma-3. On contracts, the pruned version reached 62.6% token reduction with 113,426 vocabulary entries, against 61.8% for the best in-place BPE configuration, which uses 207,803.

VocabX does not make the model smarter. It makes the model stop paying for text it does not need to write piece by piece, and stop scoring a vocabulary it will never use. In our grader, that cut measured inference cost by 77%, with the same base model and the same training recipe.

Sources indicate that specialization usually starts with data and weights. It can also start one layer earlier, in the vocabulary.

The full method, the tables for every experiment and the discarded interventions will be in the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon.

The Scaling Problem No One Talks About in Education: Who Checks the Teacher?

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1033 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

💡 Key Takeaways
  • I remember when we started discussing a major venture round to open up 30 upcoming children’s clubs a year, one investor’s question stuck with me: “How will you keep the quality of teaching the same in location number 30 as in location number one?”.
  • According to recent reports, frankly, he asked me the right question.
  • Industry observers note that most education networks control quality the way they did 30 years ago.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I remember when we started discussing a major venture round to open up 30 upcoming children’s clubs a year, one investor’s question stuck with me: “How will you keep the quality of teaching the same in location number 30 as in location number one?”.

According to recent reports, frankly, he asked me the right question. In education, scale is rarely limited by capital, real estate, or demand. It’s instead limited by the one thing that is hardest to copy: what actually happens between a teacher and a group of children when no one is checking?

Industry observers note that most education networks control quality the way they did 30 years ago. A supervisor visits the site, sits in on a class, and takes notes. Then, someone else watches a recording later. It works at three locations, but this could be broken at the last branch.

Recent findings suggest that let me explain this using GMNSM as an example. Take 10 locations, with four groups a day at each, six days a week. At 30 minutes of review per session, that adds up to 480 review hours over four weeks. Using our own staffing costs for manual reviews, I estimate that would cost about US$6,100. The estimated workload grows with every club you add. Sampling keeps that workload down, but it leaves most lessons unseen.

The lesson for education is straightforward: if you can only inspect a sliver of what happens, you are not managing quality, but guessing at it.

Speech AI has become good enough, and cheap enough, to turn a lesson recording into something a manager can act on. The research is also catching up. In a pre-registered randomized controlled trial with 224 Utah mathematics and science teachers, automated feedback on classroom audio increased teachers’ use of focusing questions by 20% compared with a control group.

Sources indicate that commercial tools are following now as well. Coverage in Education Next describes apps that separate teacher and student speech, and reports talk time and wait time, “like a Fitbit for instruction.” However, the same piece also raises the hard question: what happens when this data moves from private reflection into a formal evaluation?

At GMNSM, we built Allim AI, an internal system to automate this quality loop, and the process was more instructive than the technology.

It has been revealed that the idea is simple. You give the model your methodology – values, annual programme, lesson structure, and expected outcomes. The system reviews the coach’s speech in the discussion after practice, not the training session itself. It checks which questions the coach asked against the lesson plan and flags moments that may warrant human review. If the lesson is about building confidence, we ask: “did the coach discuss the assigned video, ask the required questions, summarize the takeaways, and help children apply them to real life?”.

The output is a score and practical coaching notes: fewer filler words, less judgemental language, and more room for different perspectives instead of one “correct” answer.

Three design decisions mattered more to us than the model itself.

Industry observers note that not everyone welcomed this in GMNSM. Some colleagues left because mandatory microphones felt like we didn’t trust them. I understand their reaction, and I would even be suspicious of any founder who dismisses it.

The wider data notes this is not an edge case. Gallup research found that only 20% of employees who work on a computer or digital device have a great deal of trust in their leaders to use employee data responsibly. A 2025 ExpressVPN survey found that one in six employees had considered quitting over monitoring they considered invasive. As one expert put it in a recent HR Daily Advisor-style analysis of AI that detects toxic managers, the same tool can look like support in a high-trust organization and “Substantial Brother” in a low-trust one.

So, my practical advice to other operators is this: treat it as a development tool first. If staff only ever see it as a scoreboard, they’ll either game it or leave. If it gives them specific, private, useful feedback, many will start using it the way it’s intended to be used. Tell people what gets recorded, why, and who sees it before it goes out. Also, accept that some people will opt out. When we did this, we explained the purpose to some colleagues and parted ways with others, which we respect.

Recording children’s classes raises obvious data-protection questions, and in Europe, the rulebook is tightening. Under the EU AI Act, certain uses of AI in education and employment can be classified as high-risk, depending on the system’s intended purpose. Not every use falls into that category, but the direction of travel is clear: the more an AI system influences decisions about people, the more scrutiny it should expect.

Sources indicate that whatever the legal classification, the practical principles are the same. Disclose what is recorded and who can access it. Minimize the data you collect. Keep people, not algorithms, responsible for decisions. These practices help earn the trust that makes feedback at scale possible.

Finally, AI will not fix a weak methodology, and it cannot replace a coach who genuinely cares about children. What it can do is make quality visible, consistently and affordably, so the lesson in location number 30 is no more of an accident than the lesson in location number one.

Andrej Kuprejev is the founder and CEO of GMNSM, a Dubai-based martial arts and holistic education network, and the founder of Allim.AI, the AI platform that supports coaching quality across its academies. A Lithuania-born former competitive judo and jiu-jitsu athlete, he founded GMNSM in 2022 to combine physical training with soft-skills development for children. It now runs 11 academies across the UAE, Qatar and Cyprus.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Cursor has traced the origins of a security incident involving a malicious version of Anthropic's Claude Code extension in its marketplace to a breach at AI infrastructure provider Fireworks.
  • It has been revealed that as many as 5,000 users may have downloaded the tampered extension during the roughly 11 hours it was live on Oct.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A compromised key issued to AI infrastructure provider Fireworks was used by threat actors to access Cursor data and credentials.

Cursor has traced the origins of a security incident involving a malicious version of Anthropic's Claude Code extension in its marketplace to a breach at AI infrastructure provider Fireworks.

It has been revealed that as many as 5,000 users may have downloaded the tampered extension during the roughly 11 hours it was live on Oct. 29. It was a reminder of the risk organizations face when they rely on third-party marketplaces for software applications and extensions. It also illustrates how one security lapse can lead to a cascade of subsequent breaches and supply chain attacks.

When Cursor first disclosed the incident, the company stated attackers had placed malicious versions of Anthropic's Claude Code extension in a cache serving its Visual Studio (VS) Code extension marketplace. Users who requested either of two specific cached versions of the extension (2.1.312 and 2.1.313) during the exposure window may have downloaded the malicious builds, the company said. The malicious extensions attempted to collect information about infected systems and establish persistent remote access, including by installing an attacker-controlled SSH key.

Related:Critical PHP Flaws Allow Code Execution, but Don't Panic 'PHP2Shell'-Style.

According to recent reports, cursor quickly removed the malicious extensions, temporarily shut down its marketplace, and audited the store for signs of further tampering. Cursor also rotated its keys, rebuilt the marketplace, and worked with the cloud provider hosting the attacker's server to take it offline. The organization's initial advisory, however, did not explain how the attacker might have gained access to its environment and planted the malicious extension in its extensions marketplace.

In an update on Nov. 13, Cursor filled in that blank, with a detailed description of what its investigation had unearthed in the days following the Oct. 29 incident.

The intrusion, according to Cursor, began when an attacker obtained an access key the company had issued to Fireworks, an AI startup based in San Mateo, Calif. Cursor said "the key was exposed by Fireworks," and the attacker used it to copy data from a read-only storage bucket containing historical coding-agent session records belonging to Cursor users. Most of the records were from 2025 and involved sessions that were not in Privacy Mode and that Cursor was permitted to use for model training purposes.

It has been revealed that some of the stored session records contained credentials that had not been properly redacted. The attacker used those credentials to access what Cursor described as select SaaS tools for accessing non-production source code repositories, customer support data, emails, usage metrics, and other data.

Related:Grok Bots Attempt to Access Corporate Data Without User Approval.

On Oct. 29, the attacker subsequently used one of the compromised credentials to tamper with the cache that Cursor uses to deliver extensions through its VS Code marketplace. The attacker inserted unauthorized copies of Anthropic's Claude Code extension in the marketplace where they remained available to users for about 11 hours.

Recent findings suggest that "Anthropic did not publish this copy, and this was not a vulnerability in Anthropic's product," Cursor stressed in its update. "The marketplace source, Open VSX, never had the malware. At most 5,000 people who requested specific cached versions of the extension on October 29 potentially received the malicious build.".

Industry observers note that cursor estimated that API credentials belonging to fewer than 0.01% of its customers were exposed in the incident. Historical coding-agent session records, or traces, belonging to fewer than 0.05% of customers were accessed, the firm mentioned.

However, the supply chain attack goes back even further than Fireworks, which itself was a victim of a third-party breach. In a Nov. 9 revision, Fireworks noted a cloud provider hosting the AI company's R&D systems "experienced a security incident on Oct. 23." The attackers used the access to the R&D systems to obtain sensitive data, including API keys and access tokens.

Related:F-Secure Identifies 26 Ways AI Can Harm Consumers, and Where to Stop Them.

According to Fireworks, the available evidence linked the breach of its environment to a financially motivated cybercriminal group seeking to monetize unauthorized access to large language models. It's a practice known as LLMjacking, which Google and others have described as a rapidly emerging threat for organizations across multiple sectors in North America, Asia-Pacific, and other regions.

It has been revealed that following the incident, Cursor said it has implemented a broad security overhaul to reduce the risk of similar compromises. Immediate steps the company has taken include cutting off Firework's access to all its shared data sets, revoking and replacing potentially exposed credentials, and rotating internal credentials. The company has also tightened restrictions on how its systems and third-party service providers can communicate with one another and expanded automated scanning for secrets across its code repositories and internal data.

The Cursor incident is another indication of how the rapid adoption of AI-powered development tools and increasingly interconnected software ecosystems has exacerbated software supply chain risks. Recently, for instance, researchers uncovered more than 550 exposed secrets in Microsoft VS Code and Open VSX extension packages, including over 100 publishing tokens that could have allowed attackers to distribute malicious updates to legitimate extensions. Similarly, earlier this year researchers identified dozens of malicious GlassWorm VS Code extensions seeded in the Open VSX marketplace to steal developer credentials that attackers could use to spread poisoned software packages.

Industry observers note that illinois-based Jai Vijayan is a veteran, award-winning technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software supply chain security, cloud security and emerging enterprise technologies.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that could childhood exposure to fluoridated water leave a lasting mark on cognition? Decades of data offer clues.

According to recent reports, could childhood exposure to fluoridated water leave a lasting mark on cognition? Decades of data offer clues.

Fluoride in community drinking water is not linked to lower adolescent IQ or poorer thinking skills later in life, a long-running US study finds.

Researchers followed a generation of Wisconsin school-leavers, examining cognitive performance from adolescence into their eighties.

Those exposed to fluoridated water did not show a consistent disadvantage compared with people whose communities had no fluoridation.

The findings address concerns that adding fluoride to drinking water to prevent tooth decay could undermine intellectual development.

Professor John Robert Warren, the study’s first author, noted:.

“Utah, Florida and many municipalities have chosen to remove fluoride from drinking water based on flawed studies that considered the IQ effects of exposure to massive doses of fluoride.

According to recent reports, because levels of fluoride added to municipal drinking water in the U.S. are so much lower, almost all prior evidence from those international studies is not relevant to U.S. public policy debates.”.

The research draws on the Wisconsin Longitudinal Study, which began with over 10,000 people who graduated from high school in 1957.

Researchers combined school IQ records with historical information about community water fluoridation and naturally occurring fluoride levels.

Following participants into old age allowed researchers to examine whether childhood exposure was associated with lasting differences in cognitive performance.

Comparing communities requires care because their residents can differ in ways that also relate to cognitive performance.

Once those background differences were taken into account, there was no consistent evidence that exposure was associated with either better or worse performance.

The same broad pattern appeared when researchers focused on people who had lived in the same county since early childhood, increasing confidence in their estimates of exposure.

Overall, the findings suggest that growing up with fluoridated community water is not associated with poorer cognitive performance in old age.

The study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (Warren et al., 2026).

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Nov 27, 2026 2 min read.
  • According to recent reports, netflix has developed Quasar, an internal tool that identifies which repositories use specific library API symbols, helping engineering teams assess the downstream impact of proposed changes before releasing them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Netflix Builds Quasar to Measure the Blast Radius of Library API Changes.

Nov 27, 2026 2 min read.

According to recent reports, netflix has developed Quasar, an internal tool that identifies which repositories use specific library API symbols, helping engineering teams assess the downstream impact of proposed changes before releasing them. The tool combines semantic code indexing with API comparisons to identify affected consumers, dependency versions, and relevant call sites across repositories.

The challenge extends beyond identifying whether an API change is incompatible. Compatibility tools can flag a removed method or changed signature, but they do not necessarily identify which applications call it. Dependency graphs show declared relationships rather than actual usage, while text searches can miss references involving inheritance, overloads, and generated code. Building every downstream consumer to validate a change can also be expensive.

Quasar architecture diagram showing the indexing and query workflow (Source: Netflix Blog Post).

Quasar indexes symbol definitions and references using the SCIP Code Intelligence Protocol, an open format for representing code relationships. Language-specific indexers submit data during CI builds, which Quasar stores in Amazon S3 as Parquet files and queries through Amazon Athena.

According to recent reports, during pull request analysis, Quasar compares API definitions between commits and identifies added, removed, or modified symbols. It then queries indexed references to locate affected repositories, dependency versions, and source locations. A Netflix example highlights a deprecated method removal affecting 137 repositories across three library versions.

Example Quasar impact report showing affected repositories and dependency versions (Source: Netflix Blog Post).

It has been revealed that however, an absence of indexed references does not prove that an API is unused. Reflection, dynamic loading, stale indexes, and incomplete coverage can prevent Quasar from observing every consumer.

Antonio J. del Águila, founder of Knaisoma, highlighted another limitation in a LinkedIn discussion about the approach:.

Observed usage has a blind spot for reflection and for code on rare paths, like a quarterly batch job, since those calls may never show up in the window that was sampled.

Roberto Pérez Alcolea, a member of Netflix's Java Platform Team and author of the original article, acknowledged the limitation and described ongoing work to complement static evidence:.

Reflection and incomplete indexing remain blind spots, and we’re also investing in runtime analysis to complement the static evidence. Together, those signals help inform removal decisions, without guaranteeing that an API is safe to delete.

Quasar complements Revapi for API compatibility analysis and Kythe for code navigation by connecting API changes with actual usage across repositories. SCIP supports usage queries across Java, Go, Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, and Rust, while compatibility analysis covers JVM APIs and Protobuf changes traced through generated Java code. Netflix exposes findings through REST, GraphQL, and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server for developers and coding agents.

Netflix plans to move impact analysis earlier into coding workflows, allowing agents to identify public API changes and retrieve consumer information before pull requests are opened. The goal is to help prepare migration changes while keeping API and release decisions with library producers.

Tech Report: Turning Database Grading into RL Rewards: Post-Training Agents with ThinkingBox

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, this is the follow up to our first blog post, The Agent Mentioned It Was Done.
  • We built ThinkingBox to evaluate an agent's work by comparing the final database state with the expected outcome.
  • Industry observers note that figure 1.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, this is the follow up to our first blog post, The Agent Mentioned It Was Done. The Database Disagreed. ThinkingBox-Training is now available on GitHub.

We built ThinkingBox to evaluate an agent's work by comparing the final database state with the expected outcome. We then used the same kind of executable signal as a reward on training tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench. For Qwen3.8-27B, average success rose from 51.70% to 60.78%, while tasks completed correctly on all twenty attempts rose from 38 to 107 with 50 GRPO steps.

Industry observers note that figure 1. ThinkingBox turns executable checks of terminal database state into rewards for post-training agents on tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench.

We built ThinkingBox to catch agents that say they are done when they are not.

Industry observers note that each of its 507 tasks in ThinkingBox-Bench (our benchmark dataset) hands an agent a real backend and a set of tools, lets it work, then checks what really changed in the database. In the first post, we caught a model closing a customer's ticket as resolved while the carrier exception behind it was still open. Nine competent-looking tool calls, one wrong database row.

Then we noticed what we had built. For most tasks, an executable check can return 1 or 0 directly from the final database state. That is not just a grader. This can be a reward function.+.

Industry observers note that so we constructed a training pool from ThinkingBox-format tasks outside the benchmark and used their executable outcomes as rewards. The catch was choosing which tasks are suitable for agent training: most tasks are either already solved or hopeless for the model in front of you, and both teach it nothing.

Difficulty is policy-relative: a task is hard for the current model only until that model learns it.

We call this offline policy-relative difficulty. We estimated each task's success probability once using the base policy before training and kept the selected training pool fixed throughout the run.

We used offline policy-relative difficulty to build the training pool, then fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B with GRPO for 50 steps. To recap, we evaluate each of the 507 benchmark tasks 20 times. pass@1 measures average success across all 10,140 attempts. pass@20 measures the share of tasks solved at least once. Observed 20/20 measures the share of tasks that pass every recorded attempt.

Table 1. Qwen3.8-27B results before and after 50 steps of GRPO on the offline-selected training pool.

In a recent development, training sharply increased repeatable success, with a small decline in at-least-once coverage. The rest of the post explains how we selected practice tasks, built the reward loop, and measured that tradeoff.

What does that improvement look like on one task? A traveler requests a room downgrade, but company policy requires manager approval first. Before training, the agent changed the booking and issued refunds without approval in 15 of 20 attempts. After RL fine-tuning, it preserved the booking and payment state in all 20.

Sources indicate that figure 2. One corporate hotel-booking task, 20 attempts per model. The base Qwen3.8-27B model changed the booking without required manager approval in 15 attempts. The RL fine-tuned model preserved booking and payment state in all 20; all expected records matched in 19.

In a hurry? The headline result is above. The implementation is in Run the training stack.

ThinkingBox-Bench grades agents on the database records they leave behind. Each of its 507 tasks starts a real backend, hands the agent a set of MCP tools and a simulated LLM user with private context, and at the end runs executable checks against the terminal database state. Checks are against the backend record that needs to be correct, not the specific tool calls. This incentivizes the model to discover possibly fresh solution paths rather than “rediscover” the human-backed solution, that might be suboptimal albeit correct.

In our first post we ran eighteen models through that benchmark twenty times each and reported a gap that headline accuracy hides. Kimi-K3 solved 93.89% of tasks at least once but completed only 68 of 507 tasks (13.41%) on all twenty recorded attempts. Claude Opus 5 inverted it: narrower coverage, far more consistency.

Sources indicate that and bigger or better model did not close it. Claude Opus 5.5 scored 0.66 percentage points higher than Claude Opus 5 on pass@1, yet passed exactly the same number of tasks, 241, on all twenty attempts. That gain in headline accuracy bought zero additional dependability.

If you are choosing a model for work that touches production database records, pass@1 should not be read alone. Observed 20/20 demonstrates which tasks succeed on every attempt, which is closer to what production reliability requires.

The executable terminal-state verdict was also the training reward. Before unpacking the training loop, here is what changed on the sealed benchmark.

After training Qwen3.8-27B, we evaluated the selected step-50 checkpoint on the 507-task benchmark it had never trained on. The 507 tasks represent an out-of-distribution test set: their domains, databases, and most MCP tools were not encountered during RL training.

Sources indicate that table 2. ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain, for selected models from our first blog's Table 2 and our fine-tuned model for different domains and overall. Observed 20/20 numbers are over the entire benchmark with 507 tasks. Each model is evaluated on all 507 tasks for 20 repeated trials. Bold marks the column leader; underline marks the runner-up.

Industry observers note that the headline result is the observed-20/20 row in Table 1. A 27B model that initially completed 38 (7.5%) of ThinkingBox-Bench on every attempt now completes 107 (21.1%) on every attempt, almost thrice. For comparison, observed 20/20 for Kimi-K3 is 68, GPT-5.4 with 128, GPT-6 Astra has 231, and Claude Opus 5.5 leads with 241.

Industry observers note that average success and repeatability produce different orderings. In Table 2, we notice that GPT-5.6 Sol scored slightly higher on pass@1 than the RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B (61.91% versus 60.78%) but passed fewer tasks on all 20 recorded attempts: 82 versus 107. Claude Sonnet 4.6 scored lower on pass@1, at 59.19%, yet passed nearly the same number of tasks every time, at 102. Neither metric alone captures the full picture.

Industry observers note that the observed pattern is consistent with sharpening: repeatable success rose while at-least-once coverage fell slightly. This is in-line with prior work. One explanation is that probability distribution moved toward trajectories that work repeatedly while some low-probability paths disappeared.

Overall, the model did not become broader. It became more repeatable. The next question is where those gains landed.

Recent findings suggest that figure 3. Domain-level base scores, RLFT scores, and percentage-point changes. Green change cells show gains and red cells show declines; blue shading indicates the score level within each metric.

Pass@1 and observed 20/20 rose in all five domains. Pass@20 was mixed: it increased in neobank and consulting, but declined in retail, travel, and auto insurance. Auto insurance had the largest breadth loss (−7.0 points), while retail had the largest observed-20/20 gain (+24.5 points).

The first post priced consistency using simple math: divide the estimated cost of the full 20-run campaign by the number of tasks the model passed every single time.

Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of the 507 × 20 campaign ÷ tasks passing 20/20.

Applying the same cost math to the fine-tuned checkpoint's measured token usage:.

Table 3. Estimated evaluation cost and dependability for base and RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B. Cost per successful attempt divides total estimated campaign cost (507 x 20) by the number of passing attempts.

At $8.00 per dependable task, the fine-tuned model came close to GPT-5.4 ($6.80), GPT-6 Astra ($7.45), and Claude Opus 5.5 ($7.80) in the companion comparison.

Figure 4 prices cost per successful attempt against pass@1.

Sources indicate that figure 4. The golden arrow traces Qwen3.8-27B base pareto cost position to the RLFT (diamond): pass@1 rises from 51.70% to 60.78% while estimated cost per successful attempt falls from $0.177 to $0.139. Ringed circles mark the Pareto cost frontier.

According to recent reports, the move places the fine-tuned checkpoint close to GPT-5.6 Sol, although GPT-5.6 Sol remains cheaper and slightly higher on pass@1. Four models priced in our paper fall outside the plotted range.

The dollar values are a comparative serving index, not invoice or cloud bills. Serving the fine-tuned checkpoint would be the same as the base model. The calculation includes model inference cost, and excludes training run and policy-probe cost for curating the training dataset.

Industry observers note that these results tell us what moved. The next sections explain the training loop and why selecting the right tasks matters the most.

Figure 5. The six stages, now in context: candidate tasks feed in, the first three run once offline, the last three repeat for every group in the training run. The trained checkpoint is evaluated against ThinkingBox-Bench.

Selection runs once, offline, against the base policy model, i.e in this case Qwen3.8 27B; training then uses that fixed pool that has been curated. The dashed amber arrow in Figure 5 marks the path we did not take: re-probing difficulty during the training run.

Every rollout is a complete episode, not a text completion. It gets a fresh backend, an isolated MCP session, and GPT-5 Chat as the simulated user. Most rewards come from deterministic terminal-state checks; a minority of narrow rubric requirements can invoke the configured judge (GPT-5 Chat).

Sources indicate that training and evaluation must interpret Qwen output identically. That includes reasoning extraction, tool calls, argument typing, rendering, and isolated task state. Otherwise the reward measures a different agent from the one evaluated. The shared interpretation code is in trainer/core/tb_interpret.py.

According to recent reports, for the reference run, we ran full-parameter RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B on 187 tasks using token-mean GRPO. Each revision generated 18 groups of 8 rollouts, or 144 episodes, across 24 H100s. Training ran synchronously with parameter and optimizer offload; AdamW used a 1e-6 learning rate and zero weight decay. We ran the training for 50 steps.

Zero-variance groups were replaced DAPO-style during training. System errors were handled separately: a backend timeout is not an incorrect agent outcome, so affected groups were refilled rather than scored as failures.

Industry observers note that that explains how retained tasks were trained. The remaining question is which tasks entered the training pool.

Before diving deep into the selection of training tasks, a disclaimer:.

It has been revealed that no ThinkingBox-Bench task was included in the RL training pool. The benchmark was reserved for evaluation.

ThinkingBox-Bench is out-of-distribution relative to the RL training pool: its domains, databases, policies, and most tools were not encountered during RL training. The two sets still share the ThinkingBox framework, simulated-user machinery, executable terminal-state grading, a few common tools, and a similar task style. These shared elements limit the scope of the transfer claim.

Why selection matters comes down to one arithmetic fact about GRPO. If all eight rollouts fail, the reward vector is [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]. If all eight succeed, it is [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]. In either case, centering within the group produces no task-reward advantage because no trajectory did better than another.++.

A mixed group such as [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1] supplies the contrast GRPO can learn from. That distinction is expensive for a stateful agent: every rollout provisions an isolated backend, runs a real tool session, and calls a separate model to play the user.

The question that shaped this work was therefore not only which model or optimizer? It was: which candidate tasks should enter the fixed training pool?

We used an offline pass-rate filter on the posterior to select the training pool. It estimates which tasks are likely to produce contrasting terminal rewards under the base policy.

Sources indicate that so we probe. Each candidate task is run repeatedly against the base policy model. The plain-language rule is simple: tasks the model always fails are unlikely to teach it yet; tasks it always passes are already learned; tasks it solves sometimes are where outcomes can provide contrast.

Recent findings suggest that each candidate task is run n times, producing k successes. We model its latent success probability with Jeffreys posterior probability:.

success probability | k successes in n probes ~ Beta(k + ½, n − k + ½).

Figure 6. Offline policy-relative difficulty is estimated from repeated base-policy probes and used to retain tasks likely to produce contrasting rewards.

According to recent reports, we partition the unit interval into five buckets with boundaries at 0.08, 0.40, 0.60, and 0.90, chosen as hyperparameters for these runs. Each task is assigned to the bucket containing the greatest posterior mass:.

Further details are in Appendix C.4 of our ThinkingBox paper.

In a recent development, figure 7. Zooming in, one task through all six stages: GPT-5.4 screening, base-model probes, difficulty classification, a rollout group, terminal-state grading, and a GRPO revision.

It has been revealed that figure 7 follows one candidate task that can potentially enter the training pool. For the Qwen3.8 27B full-parameter pool, GPT-5.4 first served as a solvability screen. The base policy then succeeded on few of the probes e.g 3 of 8, producing a Beta(3.5, 5.5) posterior. Its largest mass, 54.0%, fell in the Difficult band.

Industry observers note that when sampled for training, the task produced the mixed reward group [0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1]. Successful trajectories therefore received above-mean task advantage and failed trajectories below-mean advantage, giving GRPO contrast to learn from. A different policy model could place the same task in a different difficulty band.

The final Qwen3.8-27B curated training pool contained 187 tasks.

Nothing about the trajectory. The reward is the task's own executable verdict.

When an episode ends, the sandbox extracts what actually changed in the backend and runs the task's deterministic checks against the terminal state. Any trajectory that produces the correct end state passes. Wrong, missing, or extra side effects fail. The reward is 1 or 0.

In the benchmark, the database grader can be thought of as the “examiner”: it caught agents that reported success and left the wrong record. In training, the same kind of check can be seen as the “teacher” on a different, disjoint set of tasks.

Two reward paths, one binary verdict.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a previous post, we introduced TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium (the torch-neuronx package).
  • It has been revealed that the torch-neuronx model support Space answers that question for the most popular models on the Hub.
  • It has been revealed that the Space opens on the Selected view: our own selection of models picked among the top models on the Hub by downloads and by trending score.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a previous post, we introduced TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium (the torch-neuronx package). With it, Transformers runs its own modeling code on Trainium, as it does on any other device, so any Transformers model on the Hub may run. Which ones actually do?

It has been revealed that the torch-neuronx model support Space answers that question for the most popular models on the Hub. It tells you whether a model runs unmodified on Trainium, and gives you the script to run it yourself.

It has been revealed that the Space opens on the Selected view: our own selection of models picked among the top models on the Hub by downloads and by trending score. Each row gives the result, the number of Trainium cores the model is sharded over, the wall time of the run (compilation included) and the peak device memory.

In a recent development, to look up a given model, switch to the Trending or Downloads view and type part of its name. These views follow the Hub's own rankings, one task at a time, whether a model was tested or not. When a model was left out on purpose, the Space tells you why (most of the time it was not prioritized, sometimes it is truly incompatible). You can also pick the versions of the Neuron compiler (neuronx-cc) and of Transformers to look at.

It has been revealed that at the time of writing, only Transformers models are tested, and our selection is limited to text-generation and image-text-to-text models. We plan to expand to diffusers, sentence transformers, and other transformers tasks.

Recent findings suggest that select a model to see how to run it. The Space lists the Neuron stack the model was tested on, the packages to install on top of it, and the run.py script that ran. The script follows the recipe of the TorchNeuron announcement: it loads the model with from_pretrained, sharded when it needs to be, then generates with a static cache and torch.compile(backend="neuron").

On a Trainium2 (trn2) instance with that stack, for example in the AWS Neuron Deep Learning Container, install the packages, then run:.

No need for torchrun: the script launches its own torch.distributed ranks when the model is sharded.

According to recent reports, A first run starts by compiling the model's graphs. To skip that step, copy the graphs the same compiler built during the test, from the public NEFF cache bucket. The Space gives you the command, with the right compiler version:.

Sources indicate that each test loads the model on a trn2 instance, sharded over the smallest number of Trainium cores that can hold its weights. Most models are sharded with tensor parallelism. Mixture-of-experts models without a tensor-parallel plan use expert parallelism only. The test then generates 32 tokens and checks them. On a single core, the tokens are compared with those of a CPU run of the same checkpoint. When the model is sharded, a small judge model checks that the text is fluent English.

At the time of writing, only models that fit on 4 Trainium2 devices are tested, which means 16 cores at most. A PASS indicates nothing about throughput, or about longer generations.

Everything the Space highlights comes from the public aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support dataset, with one Parquet file per pair of neuronx-cc and library versions.

Industry observers note that each row holds a model's result, the error when it failed, the versions of the whole stack and the run.py that ran. You can query it directly:.

The dataset card gives the exact meaning of each result.

Next time you wonder whether a model runs on Trainium, look it up.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that trueLayer announced on November 27, 2026, that a Papa John’s AI agent had completed what it described as the first agentic Pay by Bank payment to a named UK retailer. The pilot involved UK retail banks including Lloyds and NatWest and ran through the Financial Conduct Authority’s Supercharged Sandbox.

According to recent reports, the agent helped with the customer’s order and then paid directly from the bank account linked to the customer’s Papa John’s account. Pay by Bank uses open-banking technology to link a bank account rather than a card, bringing the payment step into the AI-assisted ordering process. At a showcase on November 26, 2026, TrueLayer presented its findings to the FCA and industry participants.

It has been revealed that A customer creates one mandate with the bank, setting limits for a particular merchant or over a chosen period that the agent cannot exceed. Each attempted payment is checked against those limits, so an instruction above them is declined by the bank rather than relying on the agent to police itself. Payment approval remains inside the bank app, keeping banking credentials and passwords away from the agent. Customers can revoke the arrangement through either the merchant or their banking app at any time.

Recent findings suggest that this separates the agent’s ability to initiate a purchase from the bank’s enforcement of the customer’s payment authority. TrueLayer also described the pilot as the first agentic use of the variable recurring payment APIs at Lloyds and NatWest, bank interfaces for payments authorized under an ongoing customer mandate.

Recent findings suggest that trueLayer argues that bank mandates let consumers delegate purchases without sharing card details, that non-card payments can preserve competition in payment acceptance as agents handle more shopping, and that the showcase can inform the conditions and standards needed for safe adoption at scale. The work remains a sandbox pilot rather than a general consumer launch.

In a recent development, the retailer pilot followed TrueLayer’s July 22, 2026 announcement of its selection for the sandbox. The FCA received 199 applications and selected 21 companies for a cohort running from July 13, 2026, through December 31, 2026, with a particular focus on agentic payments. The sandbox, part of the FCA’s AI Lab, provides a controlled setting and regulatory support for moving advanced AI use cases toward commercial deployment.

According to recent reports, an earlier prototype kept a person in the loop while completing a transaction inside an AI shopping agent. It supported a one-off immediate payment and Bank on File, which establishes a recurring mandate for future purchases. The Papa John’s work extends those mechanics into a named retailer’s ordering flow with participating UK banks.

The FCA’s expectations for agentic AI in financial services, published on November 24, 2026, add regulatory context to the demonstration. The regulator said firms must identify which agent activities require authorization and which rules apply, particularly when software can initiate transactions, move money, arrange borrowing or make investment decisions.

In a recent development, using an external AI provider does not transfer compliance responsibility away from a regulated firm or its senior managers. They are expected to understand how autonomously their systems act, the risks created and the controls needed in real time and under stress. When customers’ agents approach a firm, it should have processes to recognize the agent, verify consent and permitted actions, and provide help if something goes wrong.

According to recent reports, payments are a specific case. Before accepting an agent’s instructions, firms should assess their systems, controls and potential liabilities, including whether to accept a payment initiated by an AI agent or from a wallet under its control. The pilot’s bank-held mandate and in-app approval address the spending-control portion of that assessment; they do not by themselves settle broader questions of regulatory authorization, liability and senior-management oversight.

According to recent reports, the pilot establishes a concrete division of authority between agent and bank. Wider adoption depends on pairing that payment mechanism with the FCA’s broader expectations for accountability, consent, liability and customer support, which extend beyond whether an individual transaction stays within its limit.

Aditya Infotech Limited said in a stock-exchange filing on November 27, 2026 that it had completed a ₹45.39 crore cash purchase of 30% of KGraph AI Solutions Private Limited on a fully diluted basis. KGraph becomes an associate manufacturer, with its BLUE video-analytics technology slated for integration into CP PLUS surveillance products.

It has been revealed that the manufacturer’s November 5, 2026 announcement described the consideration as a mix of fresh equity and purchases from existing shareholders, with an implied post-money valuation of approximately ₹151 crore. Managing Director Aditya Khemka noted: “Video compression is foundational to the next phase of surveillance. As cameras multiply and resolutions rise, the cost of storing and moving video becomes the real constraint.”.

In a recent development, the price was based on a registered valuer’s report. The transaction was not a related-party deal, none of Aditya Infotech’s promoters, promoter group or group companies had an interest in KGraph, and no governmental or regulatory approvals were required.

Recent findings suggest that KGraph’s Semantic Codec adds a perception-aware compression layer to the standard H.264 video codec, identifying redundant visual information while retaining essential details. Based on deployment data, Aditya Infotech noted the technology could reduce video storage and bandwidth requirements by up to 90%.

The codec is designed for cost-efficient edge hardware without GPU infrastructure and works with existing cameras and recording systems. The company stated this could extend video retention and lower deployment costs without replacing installed infrastructure, giving CP PLUS a potential upgrade path for customers already running surveillance equipment.

KGraph’s broader BLUE platform turns continuous video streams into searchable enterprise data. The investment is part of CP PLUS 2.0, Aditya Infotech’s move from hardware-led surveillance toward integrated security covering data management, edge computing, AI analytics and cloud integration.

KGraph will continue to operate independently while collaborating with Aditya Infotech’s R&D and engineering teams in Noida, Ahmedabad and Taiwan. The collaboration pairs KGraph’s computer-vision, embedded-systems and compression expertise with Aditya Infotech’s engineering, manufacturing and customer reach.

In a recent development, KGraph’s six co-founders bring 15 to more than 20 years of experience and academic backgrounds from IIT Bombay and IIM Bangalore. The company has a 10-patent pipeline, with three applications filed and seven in progress.

Sources indicate that incorporated on August 16, 2023, KGraph develops AI-powered software for compliance, automation, safety, monitoring and regulatory reporting across industrial and commercial sectors. It operates in India, and BLUE is its principal product. The completion filing reported audited turnover of approximately ₹80 lakh in FY2025-26, compared with approximately ₹36 lakh in FY2024-25 and no turnover in FY2023-24.

It has been revealed that aditya Infotech’s board approved the investment on November 5, when the parties executed a share subscription and purchase agreement and a shareholders’ agreement. The original transaction filing allowed 30 days from execution, or a later mutually agreed date, for completion. Closing on November 27 therefore fell within the initial timetable.

The completed stake gives CP PLUS access to KGraph’s compression and analytics expertise while leaving the startup independent. The commercial question now is whether joint engineering can turn the company-reported efficiency gains into deployed CP PLUS products and a larger revenue base for KGraph.

💡 Key Takeaways
